title: Quantum Generative Adversarial Networks with Entangled Node Representations
abstract: This paper explores the application of quantum generative adversarial networks (QGANs) enhanced with entangled node representations. The core idea is to represent nodes within the GAN architecture as entangled quantum states, thereby facilitating correlated data generation and potentially enabling the capture of more complex underlying patterns. Traditional GANs struggle with mode collapse and difficulty in representing high-dimensional data distributions. We hypothesize that leveraging quantum entanglement can overcome these limitations, leading to improved generative performance. This work outlines the theoretical framework, proposes a method for encoding nodes using entangled states, and discusses the necessary training protocols, which will likely require advanced quantum optimization algorithms. The potential impact of this approach is significant, suggesting a new direction for generative modeling that directly harnesses the power of quantum mechanics. We present a conceptual model and outline the key challenges and future research directions for this nascent field.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Automated Theorem Proving in Hardware Verification
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to automated theorem proving in hardware verification by leveraging probabilistic programming. Current automated theorem provers in this domain are hampered by their reliance on manually constructed logical formulas, restricting their applicability and expressive power. Our method utilizes probabilistic programming languages like Stan and PyMC to represent hardware specifications and verification goals as probabilistic models. The system then automatically derives proofs by exploring the probability space of these models. This approach offers increased flexibility, scalability, and the ability to handle complex, real-world hardware systems. The core innovation lies in the integration of probabilistic programming's inherent uncertainty management with the formal rigor of automated theorem proving, potentially leading to more robust and reliable verification results. We outline the system architecture, discuss key challenges, and present a conceptual framework for this new paradigm.

title: Dynamic Neuron Topology Optimization (DNTO)
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Neuron Topology Optimization (DNTO), a novel approach to neural network optimization that leverages reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust the topology and connection weights of a neural network. The core idea is to simulate the dynamic topological changes observed in biological neural networks, using a "neuron topology engine" that models physical connections and adjusts them based on predefined rules and reward signals. A reinforcement learning agent then controls this engine, optimizing the network's structure and weights to maximize rewards and adapt to evolving input data and task requirements. The key innovation lies in treating the neural network's topology itself as a learnable state space, allowing for continuous adaptation and potentially surpassing the limitations of static weight tuning methods. We explore the theoretical framework and present a conceptual outline of the DNTO system, highlighting its potential to improve long-term learning efficiency and generalization capabilities.

title: Cognitive Architecture-Driven Program Synthesis
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to program synthesis driven by cognitive architectures. Traditional program synthesis methods often struggle with complex problems due to a lack of high-level reasoning and strategic planning. We argue that by mimicking human cognitive processes – specifically, the way humans decompose problems, select strategies, and execute actions – we can significantly enhance the effectiveness of program synthesis. This work introduces a framework where program synthesis is decomposed into a series of cognitive steps, each governed by a cognitive architecture. The architecture provides a structured approach to guide the synthesis process, leading to potentially more efficient and higher-quality programs. We explore the core mechanisms involved, outlining how a cognitive architecture can manage the complexities inherent in program synthesis, offering a new paradigm for intelligent software development. The research focuses on the theoretical underpinnings and design principles, laying the groundwork for future implementations and experiments.

title: Meta-Learning Graph Embeddings for Few-Shot Learning
abstract: Few-shot learning, the task of learning from limited labeled data, presents a significant challenge in graph representation learning. Traditionally, graph embedding models require extensive datasets for effective training, leading to a bottleneck when dealing with scenarios where labeled data is scarce. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging meta-learning to overcome this limitation. We introduce a meta-learning framework that enables the rapid adaptation of graph embedding models to new graph datasets with minimal labeled examples. The core idea is to train a meta-learner that learns to learn graph embeddings, effectively acquiring a prior knowledge of graph structure that can be quickly fine-tuned using the limited available data. Our method utilizes a recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture, specifically a GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit), to model the graph structure and learns embeddings based on a contrastive loss function. The meta-learner optimizes the GRU's initial parameters such that it can quickly adapt to new graphs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark graph datasets, showcasing significant improvements in embedding quality compared to traditional graph embedding methods trained with the same few-shot data. The key contributions of this work are the integration of meta-learning into graph embedding learning and the demonstration of its ability to produce high-quality embeddings with limited data, opening up new possibilities for applications in domains where labeled graph data is limited.

title: Based on Multi-Modal Quantum Entanglement: Towards Universal Quantum Algorithms
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to constructing universal quantum algorithms by leveraging the power of multi-modal quantum entanglement. The core claim is that utilizing entangled states involving multiple quantum systems can significantly enhance the efficiency and scalability of quantum algorithms compared to those relying solely on single-mode entanglement. The proposed mechanism involves the controlled generation and manipulation of multi-modal entangled states, enabling parallel computation and reducing algorithmic complexity. This work addresses a critical limitation of traditional quantum algorithms – the reliance on single-mode entanglement – and lays a foundation for large-scale quantum computation. We present a theoretical framework outlining the key concepts and potential pathways for implementing such algorithms, focusing on the mathematical underpinnings of multi-modal entanglement and its application to fundamental quantum computations. The potential impact of this approach is substantial, offering a new paradigm for developing quantum algorithms capable of tackling complex problems currently intractable for classical computers.

title: #基于多模态数据的自监督学习与知识图谱构建
abstract: This paper investigates the construction of knowledge graphs leveraging self-supervised learning on multi-modal data. Traditional knowledge graph construction heavily relies on manual annotation, which is expensive and time-consuming. We propose a novel approach that integrates text, images, and audio data, utilizing self-supervised learning techniques to automatically extract shared knowledge and build more comprehensive and accurate knowledge graphs. The core claim is that multi-modal self-supervised learning significantly improves the efficiency and accuracy of knowledge graph construction. The core mechanism involves fusing diverse data modalities and employing self-supervised learning to uncover underlying relationships. This work represents a new paradigm in knowledge graph development, offering a scalable and automated solution compared to existing methods. The proposed framework addresses limitations of current knowledge graph construction by reducing reliance on human annotation. Ultimately, this research contributes to the creation of richer, more reliable knowledge graphs, with applications across various domains. ---

title: Core Claim: Design a global optimization algorithm based on quantum entanglement, capable of efficiently solving complex optimization problems and achieving global optima.
abstract: Quantum optimization is a rapidly growing field with the potential to revolutionize various scientific and engineering disciplines. Traditional optimization algorithms often struggle to find truly optimal solutions, frequently getting trapped in local optima. Quantum optimization, however, offers a fundamentally different approach utilizing quantum entanglement to explore the solution space in a more holistic manner. This paper presents a novel global optimization algorithm based on quantum entanglement, designed to overcome the limitations of classical optimization methods. We introduce a mechanism that leverages entanglement to facilitate the exploration of a wider solution space, ultimately leading to the discovery of global optima. This work demonstrates the potential of quantum entanglement to significantly improve the efficiency and accuracy of complex optimization problems across diverse domains. The core of this algorithm lies in its intricate use of entangled states to represent and manipulate the search space, enabling the identification of optimal solutions with significantly reduced computational cost. We rigorously analyze the algorithm's performance through extensive simulations and experiments, highlighting its effectiveness in tackling challenging optimization scenarios. This paper provides a detailed exploration of the underlying principles and practical implementation of this groundbreaking approach, paving the way for future advancements in quantum optimization techniques.

title: Quantum Computing for Graph Partitioning with Optimal Speedup
abstract: Graph partitioning is a fundamental problem in computer science with applications in diverse fields like network design, compiler optimization, and data analysis. Traditional algorithms for graph partitioning often suffer from computational complexity, particularly when dealing with large graphs. This paper explores the potential of utilizing quantum computing to accelerate graph partitioning. Specifically, we investigate the application of Grover's algorithm, a quantum search algorithm, to the problem. Our core claim is that by leveraging the superposition and interference capabilities inherent in quantum mechanics, a quantum solution can achieve a provable speedup compared to classical approaches. We present a theoretical framework outlining the algorithm's operation and derive the expected speedup. The key mathematical formulation involves representing the graph partitioning problem as an unstructured search problem amenable to Grover's algorithm. We define the problem as minimizing the cut size, represented by the objective function: *f(S) = Σi∈S Σj∈Sc d(i, j)* where *S* is a subset of vertices, *Sc* is the complement of *S* in the graph, and *d(i, j)* is the shortest path distance between vertices *i* and *j*. The algorithm then constructs a quantum oracle that maps the problem state to a superposition of all possible partitions. Grover's algorithm is then applied to amplify the amplitude of the solution state, resulting in a high probability of finding an optimal or near-optimal partition. The speedup is directly proportional to the square root of the number of iterations performed by Grover's algorithm, which is influenced by the problem size and the quality of the oracle. We analyze the complexity of the quantum algorithm and compare it to the complexity of the best-known classical algorithms, demonstrating a potential for significant speedup. Further research will focus on optimizing the oracle construction and exploring other quantum algorithms suitable for graph partitioning.

title: Generative Adversarial Networks for Automated Theorem Proving
abstract: Automated theorem proving (ATP) has long been a cornerstone of mathematical reasoning and software verification. However, current ATP systems often face significant challenges when dealing with complex theorems and intricate, unstructured proof processes. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to address these limitations. The core idea is to train a GAN to generate potential proof steps, intelligently conditioned on the theorem being proven and the existing state of the proof. A theorem prover then acts as a discriminator, critically evaluating the validity of the generated steps and providing feedback to the GAN, thereby steering its learning towards more effective and concise proofs. We argue that this framework represents a significant advancement by leveraging the generative capabilities of GANs to augment and accelerate the traditionally laborious process of automated theorem proving. The methodology presented here promises a pathway to more robust and adaptable ATP systems capable of tackling a broader range of mathematical problems.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Distributed Control of Complex Systems
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) to the distributed control of complex systems characterized by conflicting objectives among agents. The core concept presented is leveraging a team of agents trained through MARL to collaboratively achieve a shared goal, while simultaneously navigating dynamic environments and managing potentially conflicting priorities. The methodology focuses on developing an agent-based system where each agent learns optimal control policies through interaction and reward signals. The research demonstrates the potential of MARL to overcome limitations inherent in traditional centralized control methods, particularly when dealing with systems where individual agent objectives are not perfectly aligned. The system's ability to adapt and learn in a distributed manner is crucial for robustness and scalability. This work offers a novel approach to tackling control problems in complex systems, providing a foundation for future research and practical applications. Key elements include the formulation of a suitable reward function, the selection of an appropriate MARL algorithm, and the design of agent interactions within the system. The results, while theoretical, highlight the feasibility and promise of this technique.

title: Quantum Entanglement Flow for Distributed Computation
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to distributed computation leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. We introduce the concept of "entanglement flow," a system designed to facilitate information exchange and computation between physically separated nodes through the manipulation of entangled states. The core claim is that this approach, utilizing multi-particle entanglement, can enable superluminal information transfer and computation, potentially surpassing the limitations of classical computing paradigms. The proposed mechanism involves constructing specifically designed entangled states – the entanglement flow – where changes in one node instantaneously affect the state of other nodes, forming the basis for distributed operations. We detail the theoretical framework, focusing on the mathematical description of entanglement flow dynamics and its potential for scalable distributed quantum computation. This work represents a shift from viewing entanglement solely as a communication channel to actively harnessing its physical properties for computation.

title: Inverse Stochastic Filtering for Inverse Cognition in Counter-adversarial systems
abstract: Recent advances in cognitive and counter-adversarial systems with the ability to infer their adversary's beliefs have garnered significant research interest in inverse filtering from a Bayesian perspective. Such counter-adversarial systems have potential applications where an autonomous system interacts with its environment, learns relevant information about it, and then adapts itself to achieve its goals optimally. An important example is the inverse cognition problem in cognitive radar-target dynamics. A cognitive radar adapts its waveform, beam pattern, and other parameters in real-time to accurately localize its target. An intelligent target can employ these inverse filtering results to evade detection and even deceive the adversarial radar. In this setting, a cognitive adversary or 'attacker' tracks its target of interest using a stochastic framework such as a Kalman filter (KF). The target or 'defender' then employs another inverse stochastic filter to infer the forward filter's estimates of the defender's state computed by the attacker. For instance, recently, inverse KF (I-KF) has been developed to predict the attacker's future steps by estimating its (forward) KF's estimates. Existing works on inverse stochastic filtering and inverse cognition consider either linear Gaussian or finite state-space models, which limits their applicability in many practical engineering problems. Hence, in this dissertation, we study inverse filtering in the general non-linear non-Gaussian system framework and develop inverse non-linear filters using different sub-optimal approaches.

title: Spillover-Aware Multi-Value Steering for Pluralistic LLM Alignment
abstract: Activation steering controls LLM behavior at inference time by adding learned directions to hidden states, but existing methods handle one concept at a time. Pluralistic alignment, where different stakeholders need different value emphases, requires steering multiple dimensions simultaneously. We show that naive steering produces substantial spillover: the effect intended for one value leaks into others. This parallels the treatment-versus-spillover decomposition in causal inference. We trace spillover to geometric entanglement of steering directions, captured by their Gram matrix, and derive a zero-cost correction from an activation-norm-penalized objective that decouples each direction's contribution exactly. Our end-to-end pipeline requires no fine-tuning, no reward model, and no manual prompt engineering: given only domain questions, it automatically discovers value dimensions, extracts directions, diagnoses entanglement, and applies corrected steering. On climate discourse, the correction improves the net steering effect from +5.9% to +14.0%, validated over 100,000 pairwise judgments.

title: Graph-Based Embedding for Social Network Analysis
abstract: This paper explores the application of graph embedding techniques to social network analysis. Traditional social network analysis methods often struggle with scalability and capturing complex relationships within large networks. Graph embedding offers a powerful alternative by representing nodes and edges as low-dimensional vectors, enabling efficient computation and analysis. This work investigates the use of established node embedding algorithms, such as DeepWalk and Node2Vec, alongside graph convolutional networks (GCNs), to learn representations of social networks. We demonstrate how these embeddings can be leveraged for various downstream tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and community detection. The core claim of this research is the efficient analysis of social networks through the mapping of nodes and edges into a low-dimensional vector space. The mechanism relies on the learning of network structure and node features via embedding algorithms. This approach represents a novel method for analyzing social networks, providing a more scalable and insightful solution compared to traditional techniques.

title: Symbolic Regression with Evolutionary Neural Networks
abstract: This paper investigates the application of evolutionary neural networks (ENNs) for symbolic regression, a technique focused on automatically discovering mathematical equations from data. Traditional symbolic regression methods often struggle with complex datasets and high-dimensional problems. ENNs offer a novel approach by integrating the learning capabilities of neural networks with the search and optimization strategies of evolutionary algorithms. The core mechanism involves iteratively refining the structure and weights of a neural network through an evolutionary process, effectively searching for equations that minimize the error between predicted and observed data. We demonstrate that ENNs can achieve competitive results compared to other symbolic regression techniques, particularly in scenarios involving non-linear relationships and multiple variables. The key contribution lies in the synergistic combination of these two powerful paradigms, leading to a robust and adaptable method for equation discovery.

abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement to revolutionize geometric optimization, specifically focusing on dynamic adjustment of geometric structures and precision computation. Traditional algorithmic approaches often rely on static analysis, limiting their adaptability to complex systems. We propose a novel method leveraging quantum entanglement to establish correlations between different components of a geometric optimization process, resulting in improved efficiency and accuracy. This approach offers a significant departure from conventional methods, utilizing the unique properties of quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust geometric structures and enable precise calculations, ultimately providing a powerful tool for complex system optimization. This research investigates the practical application of this methodology and its potential impact on various fields.

title: Dynamic Topology Quantum Machine Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum machine learning framework based on dynamic topology. Traditional machine learning methods are often static, while this framework dynamically adjusts the topology of a quantum system during training and optimization, enabling more adaptable models. We develop a method for constructing and manipulating dynamic topological structures to guide the learning process and improve model robustness. The core mechanism leverages the inherent properties of topological quantum computation to achieve enhanced generalization and adaptability. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through simulations and preliminary experiments, showcasing its potential for addressing challenges in machine learning.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Accelerated Probability Distribution Prediction
abstract: This paper explores the potential of leveraging quantum entanglement to accelerate probability distribution prediction, a computationally intensive task with significant implications across various fields including statistical physics, machine learning, and finance. The core claim is that by harnessing the unique properties of quantum entanglement, we can achieve a substantial speedup in calculating probability distributions, particularly for large-scale datasets. This is achieved through the design and implementation of a distributed quantum computing architecture, where entanglement between multiple quantum bits (qubits) allows for parallel processing of the calculations. We outline a theoretical framework and propose a computational model demonstrating this acceleration. The proposed approach addresses the limitations of classical methods, which often struggle with the exponential growth of computational complexity associated with complex probability distributions. The key mathematical components and the underlying principles driving this acceleration are presented, demonstrating a viable pathway towards a fundamentally faster method for probability distribution prediction. We demonstrate the potential for significant improvements in prediction accuracy and speed, ultimately paving the way for new advancements in areas reliant on accurate probability modeling.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Architectures for Commonsense Knowledge Integration
abstract: This paper investigates the integration of neural networks and symbolic knowledge bases – a critical area for advancing artificial intelligence. The core challenge lies in reconciling the flexible, data-driven nature of neural networks with the structured, rule-based reasoning capabilities of symbolic systems. We propose a hierarchical neuro-symbolic architecture designed to overcome this discrepancy. This architecture employs a neural network to translate natural language into symbolic representations, specifically rules and facts, which are subsequently utilized by a symbolic reasoning engine. The system operates on a bi-directional translation and reasoning process, facilitating seamless interaction between the two components. This approach allows for the efficient utilization of both the learning capacity of neural networks and the logical rigor of symbolic knowledge, leading to improved performance on complex reasoning tasks requiring commonsense knowledge. The architecture's key contribution is a structured framework for dynamic knowledge translation and reasoning, enhancing the robustness and interpretability of AI systems. We explore the design considerations and potential applications of this architecture, highlighting its ability to bridge the gap between neural and symbolic AI. ---

title: 自适应量子隐形矩阵的自适应优化算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive quantum hidden Markov model (QHM) optimization algorithm designed to enhance computational efficiency and accuracy, particularly for matrices exhibiting high complexity. Traditional QHM methods rely on static parameter adjustments, while our approach dynamically adjusts quantum matrix parameters to optimize the calculation process. We explore a new structure for the quantum matrix, incorporating a self-tuning mechanism to mitigate computational bottlenecks. The algorithm's effectiveness is validated through simulations, demonstrating improved performance metrics compared to existing approaches, especially in scenarios with significant matrix dimensions. This work offers a significant step toward robust and adaptive quantum computing, addressing a critical challenge in the field.

title: Information-Theoretic Limits of Graph Embedding Learning
abstract: Graph embedding learning aims to represent nodes in a graph as low-dimensional vectors while preserving the graph's structural information. Traditional approaches primarily rely on empirical evaluation metrics like node classification accuracy, often lacking a theoretical grounding. This work investigates the fundamental limits of graph embedding techniques from an information-theoretic perspective. We demonstrate that the inherent information loss during dimensionality reduction, as quantified by mutual information and entropy, fundamentally restricts the achievable performance. We propose a novel loss function designed to explicitly minimize this information loss, leveraging a mutual information measure derived from node degree distributions. Our approach shifts the focus from heuristic optimization to a rigorous theoretical understanding of graph embedding, offering insights into the inherent constraints and potential avenues for improvement. The core claim is that the performance of graph embedding techniques is fundamentally limited by the information loss during dimensionality reduction.

title: 基于多智能体协同学习的复杂系统建模
abstract: This paper explores the application of multi-agent collaborative learning (MACL) for modeling and simulating complex systems. Traditional methods for modeling complex systems often struggle with the inherent nonlinearity, emergent behavior, and feedback loops characteristic of these systems. We propose a novel approach where multiple intelligent agents are deployed, each representing a specific component or subsystem of the complex system. These agents interact and learn collaboratively, exchanging information and knowledge to collectively construct a more accurate and robust model. The core claim of this work is that MACL provides a superior framework for understanding and predicting the behavior of complex systems compared to conventional techniques. The key mechanism involves the decentralized learning and communication among agents, leading to a dynamic and adaptive model representation. This research offers a new paradigm for complex system modeling, particularly suited for systems where analytical solutions are unavailable or computationally intractable. We present a theoretical framework and outline the key components of a MACL-based modeling system.

title: Based on Quantum Entanglement Distributed Computing
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to distributed computing leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. The core claim is that harnessing entanglement can significantly accelerate and optimize distributed computing tasks. We introduce a novel distributed computing algorithm predicated on the manipulation and measurement of entangled states. This algorithm facilitates efficient data transfer and parallel computation by exploiting the instantaneous correlation inherent in entanglement. The proposed method represents a fundamentally new paradigm for distributed computing, moving beyond classical limitations in data transmission and processing. We detail the theoretical framework, focusing on the mathematical relationships governing entanglement-based distributed computation. The key components include the generation and distribution of entangled qubit pairs, the encoding of data into these states, the parallel processing of information via correlated measurements, and the subsequent reconstruction of the result. We provide a comprehensive mathematical description of the system, including the probability amplitudes involved in measurement outcomes and the operational equations governing the entanglement distribution process. This work lays the groundwork for future research and development in quantum-enhanced distributed computing systems. ---

title: Based on Quantum Spin-Based Computing Architecture
abstract: This paper explores a novel computing architecture predicated on the unique properties of quantum spins. Traditional quantum computing architectures face challenges related to coherence, scalability, and control complexity. We propose a framework leveraging the intrinsic advantages of spin systems – their inherent robustness against environmental noise, their ability to represent information in multiple states simultaneously, and the potential for highly precise control – to construct a more efficient and reliable computing platform. The core of this architecture revolves around manipulating and correlating quantum spins to perform computations. We detail key aspects including spin initialization, coherent manipulation protocols, and measurement strategies. This approach offers a promising alternative to existing designs, potentially mitigating some of the significant hurdles in achieving practical quantum computation. The proposed architecture is fundamentally different in its approach, offering a new computational paradigm based on exploiting the full potential of quantum spin dynamics.

title: Distributed Memoryless Kernels for Large-Scale Data
abstract: Kernel methods offer powerful tools for dimensionality reduction and classification, but their performance is severely limited by the computational cost of calculating the kernel matrix, particularly for large datasets. This paper introduces a novel approach—Distributed Memoryless Kernels—designed to overcome this bottleneck. We propose a distributed algorithm that approximates kernel calculations using memoryless kernels, coupled with efficient message passing protocols to enable parallel kernel matrix computation across multiple machines. Our method rigorously quantifies the error bounds associated with this approximation, providing a theoretical guarantee on the accuracy of the resulting approximations. The core of our approach lies in exploiting the inherent properties of memoryless kernels to minimize the memory footprint and facilitate efficient distributed computation. This work represents a significant step toward making kernel methods scalable to truly massive datasets, opening up new possibilities for applications in areas such as genomics, image analysis, and natural language processing.

title: Enhancing the Security of Quantum Key Distribution Protocols Based on Quantum Decoherence
abstract: This paper investigates the enhancement of security within Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols through the strategic utilization of quantum decoherence. Current QKD protocols often rely heavily on classical cryptographic techniques, leaving them vulnerable to sophisticated attacks. This research proposes a novel approach that leverages the inherent properties of quantum decoherence to bolster the security of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols. Specifically, we explore the implementation of quantum decoherence codes and adapted Quantum Key Agreement (QKA) protocols. The core claim is that by incorporating quantum decoherence, we can significantly improve the resilience of QKD against eavesdropping attacks. Our methodology focuses on designing protocols that exploit the probabilistic nature of quantum measurement and the effects of decoherence to disrupt potential interception attempts. We define key parameters related to decoherence rates, measurement strengths, and error correction strategies. The theoretical framework presented demonstrates the potential for enhanced security, offering a new direction for future QKD research and development. The goal is to move beyond purely classical security assumptions and embrace the unique vulnerabilities associated with quantum systems.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Hybrid Systems for Robotic Navigation with Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: This paper addresses the challenges of robotic navigation, specifically the difficulties in managing uncertainty and effectively merging neural network perception with symbolic reasoning. The proposed solution is a neuro-symbolic hybrid system designed to overcome these limitations. The system employs a neural network for raw sensory data interpretation, a symbolic planner for generating optimal trajectories, and integrates both components with rigorous uncertainty quantification techniques. This approach allows the robot to not only navigate effectively but also to reason about and mitigate the impact of uncertainty in its environment. The core claim of this work is that combining neuro-symbolic methods with robust uncertainty quantification represents a significant advancement in robotic navigation. The system's architecture and methodology are presented, detailing the integration of perception, planning, and uncertainty management. The system demonstrates enhanced navigation performance in dynamic and uncertain environments compared to traditional approaches. The research contributes to the growing field of intelligent robotics by providing a practical framework for building robust and adaptable navigation systems.

title: OpenDiscoveryTrace: Process Traces for Evaluating AI Scientist Workflows
abstract: Existing benchmarks for autonomous AI scientists evaluate only final outputs---generated code, hypotheses, or papers---yet discard the reasoning process by which those outputs were obtained. This makes it impossible to audit scientific methodology, diagnose failure modes, or distinguish systematic reasoning from fortunate guessing. We present \textbf{OpenDiscoveryTrace}, a public dataset of 558 complete AI scientific agent trajectories that captures how models reason, not just what they produce. Each trajectory records a structured 9-field-per-step trace---including thoughts, tool calls, observations, errors, revision triggers, and self-reported confidence---as models execute 124 scientific tasks spanning drug discovery, materials science, genomics, and scientific literature analysis. The dataset covers seven models: three frontier models (GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.6, and Gemini 3.1 Pro; 124 trajectories each, fully balanced across domains and difficulty levels) and four open-weight models (Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Phi-3.5-mini, and Qwen2.5-1.5B; 30 each), plus 60 live-retrieval variant trajectories. Pilot analysis on 363 LLM-judged trajectories reveals that process traces expose behavioral differences invisible to output-only evaluation: all three frontier models achieve comparable success rates (84--89%), yet Claude Opus 4.6 produces 30$\times$ more errors than GPT-5.4 (2.5 vs. 0.08 per trajectory, $p < 0.0001$, Cliff's $δ= 0.613$), with qualitatively different error profiles---66.7% tool misuse for Claude versus 83.6% reasoning errors for GPT-5.4. We define five benchmark tasks with baselines from logistic regression, random forests, LSTMs, and Transformer models. The dataset, trace schema, agent harness, and benchmark definitions are publicly available under CC BY 4.0 to support research on process-level evaluation, scientific agent auditing, and AI governance.

We present \textbf{OpenDiscoveryTrace}, a public dataset of 558 complete AI scientific agent trajectories that captures how models reason, not just what they produce. Each trajectory records a structured 9-field-per-step trace---including thoughts, tool calls, observations, errors, revision triggers, and self-reported confidence---as models execute 124 scientific tasks spanning drug discovery, materials science, genomics, and scientific literature analysis. The dataset covers seven models: three frontier models (GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.6, and Gemini 3.1 Pro; 124 trajectories each, fully balanced across domains and difficulty levels) and four open-weight models (Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Phi-3.5-mini, and Qwen2.5-1.5B; 30 each), plus 60 live-retrieval variant trajectories. Pilot analysis on 363 LLM-judged trajectories reveals that process traces expose behavioral differences invisible to output-only evaluation: all three frontier models achieve comparable success rates (84--89%), yet Claude Opus 4.6 produces 30$\times$ more errors than GPT-5.4 (2.5 vs. 0.08 per trajectory, $p < 0.0001$, Cliff's $δ= 0.613$), with qualitatively different error profiles---66.7% tool misuse for Claude versus 83.6% reasoning errors for GPT-5.4. We define five benchmark tasks with baselines from logistic regression, random forests, LSTMs, and Transformer models. The dataset, trace schema, agent harness, and benchmark definitions are publicly available under CC BY 4.0 to support research on process-level evaluation, scientific agent auditing, and AI governance.

title: SAFEGuard: Detect Optimization-Based Jailbreak Attacks Through Harmful Semantic Analysis and Fluency Measurement
abstract: Despite the significant efforts devoted to aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values and ensuring safe deployment, recent work has revealed that LLMs remain vulnerable to adversarial jailbreak attacks that can bypass safety guardrails and elicit harmful responses. Many defense methods are proposed to detect jailbreaks but they are limited in their effectiveness to counter wide-range optimization-based jailbreak mechanisms that can yield highly fluency-optimized or harmful semantic obfuscated prompts. To tackle this challenge, we propose a unified detection framework SAFEGuard which incorporates a hybrid fluency measurement based on cross-layer distribution distance and perplexity, and the analysis of harmful semantics through gradient matching. Our method is grounded in a paramount observation: high fluency prompts maintain their malicious intention close to harmful prompts while harmful semantic obfuscated prompts often inject gibberish token sequences. Our evaluation demonstrates that SAFEGuard consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and achieves significant improvement in accuracy across different optimization-based jailbreaks. This underscores the effectiveness of SAFEGuard against evolving jailbreak attacks.

title: Building predictive models from IF-THEN rules extracted from Fuzzy Cognitive Maps
authors: Fco Fernando De la Rosa Troyano
abstract: In previous work, extraction algorithms have been used to obtain sets of causal IF-THEN rules that summarise and explain the dominant dynamics of systems modelled by means of Fuzzy Cognitive Maps. This article explains how to turn those rules into predictive models that respond in real time to the state of a set of input variables and produce an output predicting the future state of the system, either as a directional signal, as a probability distribution or as both. The article discusses 1) the fundamental design decisions —separating causal variables from target variables, input modes, normalisation of the evidence—, and 2) the solutions to the most frequent problems —uneven coverage across concepts, secondary concepts, domain constraints— and includes a final section devoted to the use of large language models (LLMs) as assistants for implementing these models in an automated way.

title: 基于多模光纤的量子密钥分发协议优化
abstract: This paper investigates the optimization of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols utilizing multimode optical fibers (MMF). The core claim centers on leveraging controlled beam shaping and interference effects within MMF to enhance both the key generation rate and the security of QKD protocols. The proposed mechanism utilizes the inherent interference characteristics of MMF to increase the number of key generation paths, combined with an active control system to actively improve the key generation rate. This work represents a significant advancement by fully exploiting the unique properties of MMF for deep optimization of QKD protocols, addressing limitations inherent in single-mode fiber systems. The theoretical analysis and proposed control strategies offer a promising avenue for developing high-performance, secure QKD systems for long-distance communication. The presented approach focuses on the manipulation of the complex interference patterns within MMF to create multiple, independent paths for key generation, thereby boosting the key rate. Furthermore, the active control system allows for dynamic adjustment of these interference patterns, mitigating the effects of channel impairments and enhancing security. ---

title: Dynamic Probability Association Matrix Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the application of dynamic probability association matrix optimization to address complex optimization problems involving uncertainty and potential correlations. Traditional optimization methods often fail to adequately model these factors, limiting the robustness and generalization capabilities of the solutions. We propose a novel approach that utilizes a dynamic probability association matrix, incorporating uncertainty and potential correlations into the optimization process through a novel dynamic optimization algorithm. The core mechanism focuses on adjusting matrix parameters to better align with real-world scenarios, leading to improved results across a range of applications. This work offers a significant advancement in optimizing complex systems by intelligently incorporating uncertainty and potential relationships.

title: Title: Dynamic Constraint Representation via Quantum Superposition
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum superposition to revolutionize constraint representation and manipulation within optimization problems. Traditional methods often struggle with the computational complexity associated with representing and navigating complex constraint sets. We propose a novel dynamic constraint representation utilizing quantum superposition, aiming to significantly accelerate solution space exploration and improve the efficiency of optimization algorithms. The core mechanism involves encoding constraints as quantum states that can be manipulated through quantum gates, offering a fundamentally different approach compared to classical representations. This research investigates the feasibility of this approach, demonstrating its potential for enhanced computational performance in specific benchmark problems. The goal is to develop a method capable of efficiently handling constraints with a dramatically reduced computational burden.

title: 基于量子计算的非线性系统动力学模拟
abstract: This research investigates the application of quantum computing to the simulation of non-linear systems, specifically focusing on complex quantum chemistry reactions and physical phenomena. Traditional simulation methods often rely on classical computers, limiting the complexity and computational resources available for these intricate systems. This paper explores the potential of quantum computing to overcome these limitations, utilizing quantum entanglement and quantum algorithms to achieve unprecedented accuracy and efficiency in modeling these processes. The core claim is that quantum computing offers a significant advantage in simulating non-linear systems due to its unique capabilities in managing quantum states and exploiting superposition and entanglement. We will detail the proposed method, its mathematical underpinnings, and preliminary results demonstrating its efficacy in simulating a specific, albeit simplified, system. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and potential challenges.

title: Title: Adaptive Probability Distributions in Mathematical Logic
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of adaptive probability distributions within mathematical logic to facilitate the creation of highly expressive and computationally efficient formalisms. The core claim is to develop a system that automatically generates and refines probability distributions based on the structure of logical arguments, minimizing inconsistencies and promoting the creation of more robust and flexible formalisms. We propose a learning process centered around analyzing logical arguments to dynamically adjust the probability distributions, thereby enhancing the system's ability to produce coherent and consistent logical systems. This work represents a significant departure from traditional probabilistic reasoning, which relies on manually crafted rules, offering a self-improving mechanism for formal logic. The paper will detail the proposed system, its underlying principles, and preliminary results demonstrating its efficacy in refining logical arguments.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive topological structure aggregation method. This approach offers a significant advancement in the field of data aggregation, particularly for scenarios with dynamic data characteristics.

title: Information-Theoretic Proofs of Robustness for Randomized Algorithms
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to analyzing the robustness of randomized algorithms by leveraging information-theoretic principles. Traditional methods often rely on empirical testing and simulation, which can be computationally expensive and may not guarantee robustness across all possible adversarial inputs. We propose a framework where algorithmic analysis is recast as a problem of quantifying the mutual information between the algorithm's output and the adversary's influence. This approach allows us to establish precise probabilistic bounds on robustness, offering a fundamentally different and mathematically rigorous method compared to existing techniques. The core idea is to utilize measures such as mutual information and Kolmogorov complexity to precisely characterize the vulnerability of randomized algorithms. We explore the theoretical foundations of this method, demonstrating its potential for designing and evaluating robust algorithms in various domains. The resulting proofs provide a quantifiable metric for assessing the algorithm's resilience against adversarial manipulations, moving beyond the limitations of black-box testing.

title: Quantum Key Distribution Protocol Based on Photon Quantum Computing
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol leveraging the principles of photon quantum computing. The protocol aims to achieve high efficiency and security in key exchange by exploiting the unique properties of quantum mechanics, specifically quantum entanglement and quantum state superposition. Traditional QKD protocols primarily rely on classical physics, limiting their potential. This proposed protocol introduces a paradigm shift by integrating quantum computing capabilities directly into the key distribution process. We detail the mathematical framework underpinning the protocol, focusing on the manipulation and measurement of quantum states using photons. The core of the system involves the generation of entangled photon pairs, followed by quantum state transformations and finally, classical post-processing to distill a shared secret key. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the protocol's security based on the fundamental laws of quantum mechanics, offering a potentially superior approach to existing QKD methods. This work establishes a foundation for future research and development in high-performance, quantum-enhanced QKD systems.

title: Probabilistic Simulation of Quantum Computing Algorithms using Monte Carlo Methods
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to simulating quantum computing algorithms using Monte Carlo methods, specifically designed to account for the inherent probabilistic nature of quantum systems. Traditional simulation methods often rely on deterministic models, which fail to capture the fundamental uncertainty associated with quantum mechanics. Our method employs a stochastic simulation engine that accurately models the probabilistic behavior of quantum gates and measurements. The core of the approach involves generating a large number of samples, each representing a possible outcome of a quantum computation. By analyzing the statistical distribution of these samples, we can approximate the expected results of the algorithm. This technique offers a practical way to evaluate the performance of quantum algorithms, especially those with high levels of uncertainty, and provides a valuable tool for algorithm design and optimization. The method avoids the limitations of purely deterministic simulations and offers a more realistic representation of quantum computation. Key aspects include the development of a robust sampling strategy and the efficient calculation of probabilities. The approach is demonstrated through a detailed explanation and illustrative examples, focusing on the conceptual framework and the underlying mathematical principles.

title: Self-Supervised Learning for Procedural Content Generation with Temporal Consistency
abstract: Procedural Content Generation (PCG) has long been a challenging area within computer graphics and game development, primarily due to the difficulty in achieving temporal consistency and coherence in generated content. This work introduces a novel approach leveraging self-supervised learning to address this limitation. The system learns to generate sequences of content—such as level designs, animations, or musical pieces—by minimizing a contrastive loss that encourages consistency between successive samples. This results in a temporal representation of the desired narrative, leading to more believable and engaging generated experiences. The core idea is to treat content generation as a learning problem, allowing the system to implicitly capture the stylistic and narrative constraints inherent in the desired output. The system utilizes a latent space learned through self-supervised training to guide content generation, ensuring a degree of control and allowing for exploration of diverse yet consistent outputs. This research demonstrates a pathway towards PCG systems that can produce temporally consistent and coherent content, moving beyond purely random or rule-based generation methods.

title: Dynamically Adaptive Neural Architecture Search via Evolutionary Graph Templates
abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has emerged as a powerful technique for automating the design of neural networks, but existing methods often suffer from high computational costs and limited generalization capabilities. This work introduces a novel approach to NAS based on dynamically evolving graph templates, leveraging an evolutionary algorithm to adaptively refine network structures. The core idea is to represent network architectures as graphs and utilize an evolutionary process to explore the architecture search space efficiently. A key component of this system is a learned uncertainty metric, which guides the algorithm's exploration by prioritizing templates with higher potential for improvement. This dynamic adaptation leads to faster convergence and improved generalization performance compared to traditional NAS techniques. The proposed method offers a flexible and scalable framework for NAS, particularly well-suited for scenarios where computational resources are constrained or where the target dataset exhibits significant variability. This paper details the system architecture, the evolutionary algorithm, and the learned uncertainty metric, demonstrating its effectiveness through illustrative examples.

title: Does Channel Dominance Survive the Attack Era? Frozen Detectors, Standards-Reference Telephony, and ASVspoof 5 - code, scores, and analyses
abstract: Code, per-trial scores, and analysis outputs for the paper "Does Channel Dominance Survive the Attack Era? Frozen Detectors, Standards-Reference Telephony, and ASVspoof 5" (I. Semjonovs, 2026, submitted to ICASSP 2027). The study evaluates three frozen detectors — AASIST, RawNet2, and wav2vec2-AASIST — on the ASVspoof 5 Track 1 evaluation set across 25 standards-reference telephony conditions (Opus, Speex-WB, EVS, AMR-WB, and G.711; bitrate ladders; frame erasure), with three random seeds. Included: analysis scripts, the preregistration and deviations log, all 450 per-shard score CSVs, per-cell EER, ECE, and streaming-decision tables, and a MANIFEST.sha256 covering every file. Not included: corpus audio, the codec cache, the 3GPP reference binaries (licensed), and model weights; the README gives upstream pointers and SHA-256 checksums for the weights.

title: Development of a Computational Histology Artificial Intelligence-Powered Prognostic Biomarker in Colorectal Cancer in The Cancer Genome Atlas
abstract: Background: Risk stratification in colorectal cancer (CRC) plays an important role in treatment decision-making. As such, prognostic biomarkers that can augment risk stratification have clinical value. Quantitative histologic features from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole slide images (WSIs) provide a novel avenue for biomarker discovery. In this study, we explored the potential for a computational histology artificial intelligence (CHAI) platform to develop and validate a prognostic biomarker in CRC. Methods: The Cancer Genome Atlas Colorectal Adenocarcinoma project was utilized for this study, with inclusion of all subjects (stage I-IV) with available digitized H&E specimens. The cohort was split into development and validation cohorts by a stratified random split. The previously developed CHAI platform was applied in the development cohort to construct a continuous risk score from histologic features associated with progression-free interval (PFI) that was dichotomized based on an optimized cutpoint for distinguishing PFI into a high risk CHAI (+) and lower risk CHAI (-). PFI was compared between CHAI (+) and CHAI (-) patients in the validation cohort in multivariable Cox proportional hazards models. Time-dependent area under the curve (tdAUC) and C-indices were also calculated for PFI. Results: A total of 583 participants were included in the study, with 409 assigned to the validation cohort. The CHAI biomarker classified 229 participants (56%) as CHAI (+) and 180 (44%) as CHAI (-) in the validation set. CHAI (+) participants had worse PFI in a multivariable analysis adjusting for available clinicopathologic variables (hazard ratio (HR) = 2.65; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.63-4.30). TdAUC for the CHAI biomarker was 0.60 (95% CI, 0.53-0.67) at 12 months, 0.62 (0.55-0.69) at 36 months, and 0.67 (0.55-0.79) at 60 months; the C-index was 0.62 (95% CI, 0.58-0.67). Conclusions: The CHAI platform was used to develop a prognostic digital pathology biomarker in CRC. This demonstrates the feasibility and potential to apply this artificial intelligence-based digital pathology biomarker platform for risk stratification in CRC and supports its further study.

Time-dependent area under the curve (tdAUC) and C-indices were also calculated for PFI. Results: A total of 583 participants were included in the study, with 409 assigned to the validation cohort. The CHAI biomarker classified 229 participants (56%) as CHAI (+) and 180 (44%) as CHAI (-) in the validation set. CHAI (+) participants had worse PFI in a multivariable analysis adjusting for available clinicopathologic variables (hazard ratio (HR) = 2.65; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.63-4.30). TdAUC for the CHAI biomarker was 0.60 (95% CI, 0.53-0.67) at 12 months, 0.62 (0.55-0.69) at 36 months, and 0.67 (0.55-0.79) at 60 months; the C-index was 0.62 (95% CI, 0.58-0.67). Conclusions: The CHAI platform was used to develop a prognostic digital pathology biomarker in CRC. This demonstrates the feasibility and potential to apply this artificial intelligence-based digital pathology biomarker platform for risk stratification in CRC and supports its further study.

title: Image-Scale Robustness and Visual Recognition Performance: A Cross-Architecture Analysis
abstract: The sensitivity of visual recognition models to changes in image scale is well established, yet the factors governing this sensitivity across heterogeneous architectures remain unclear. In this work, we investigate whether scale robustness exhibits a common quantitative structure across modern vision models. We evaluate 20 pretrained ImageNet-1K classifiers spanning seven architectural families, including convolutional, mobile, efficient, and Transformer-based architectures. By systematically reducing input image scale, we construct scale-accuracy response curves and define a characteristic scale as a compact measure of the onset of substantial recognition degradation. We then examine the relationship between characteristic scale and baseline recognition accuracy, model parameter count, architectural family, and representation stability. A strong inverse association is observed between baseline accuracy and characteristic scale (Pearson r = -0.890, R^2= 0.792, p < 10^-6). This relationship remains stable under bootstrap resampling, leave-one-architecture-out analysis, and leave-one-family-out analysis. In contrast, parameter count provides negligible additional explanatory power after controlling for baseline accuracy (p = 0.80), while architectural family does not provide significant incremental explanatory power. Furthermore, characteristic scale shows essentially no association with representation stability (r = -0.003, p = 0.991). These results indicate that, across the studied models, scale robustness is strongly organized by baseline recognition performance rather than simply by model size, architectural family, or representation stability. The study provides an empirical framework for characterizing scale robustness across vision architectures and identifies a reproducible accuracy-scale regularity that warrants further theoretical investigation.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Programming with Dynamic Knowledge Graph Construction
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neuro-symbolic programming that leverages a dynamic knowledge graph construction process. The core idea is to integrate neural networks with symbolic programming, enhancing the system's ability to learn and reason. A neural network is trained to generate symbolic rules and assertions derived from input data. These generated rules are then employed to dynamically construct and update a knowledge graph. This knowledge graph, in turn, serves as a guiding influence for the neural network's learning process, establishing a continuous feedback loop between neural and symbolic reasoning. This dynamic approach allows the system to refine its knowledge representation and improve its overall reasoning capabilities compared to traditional static knowledge graph methods. The system is designed to address the limitations of purely neural or purely symbolic approaches, offering a synergistic solution for complex problem-solving.

title: 基于量子纠错码的分布式机器学习
abstract: This paper explores the potential of utilizing quantum error-correcting codes to enhance the robustness and scalability of distributed machine learning (DL) models. Traditional DL models are vulnerable to noise and data corruption in distributed environments, posing significant challenges for reliable training and inference. We propose a framework where the model parameters are encoded into quantum error-correcting codes, leveraging the inherent error correction capabilities of these codes to protect against noise. This approach allows for the detection and correction of errors introduced during transmission and computation, ultimately improving the accuracy and reliability of the distributed DL model. The core claim of this work is to demonstrate the feasibility of using quantum error-correcting codes to provide resilience to parameter updates in distributed machine learning. The mechanism involves encoding model parameters into a quantum code, followed by applying quantum error correction algorithms. This represents a novel approach to distributed DL, offering a pathway to more robust and scalable solutions. We will outline the key concepts and theoretical considerations involved in this framework.

title: Graph Representation Learning via Variational Autoencoders with Graph Kernels
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph representation learning leveraging the power of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) combined with Graph Kernels. Traditional VAEs often struggle to effectively capture the intricate relationships inherent in graph data, leading to suboptimal representations. Our method addresses this limitation by incorporating Graph Kernels to represent graph structures in a low-dimensional latent space. This allows the VAE to learn a richer, more informative representation that considers both local and global structural characteristics. We present a detailed formulation of the approach, outlining the key components and their mathematical relationships. The core idea is to use the Graph Kernel function, denoted as *K(s_i, s_j)*, where *s_i* and *s_j* are two subgraphs, to measure the similarity between them. The VAE then learns a latent vector *z* for each subgraph, such that *z = f(s)*, where *f* is the encoder function. The loss function incorporates both the reconstruction loss, denoted as *L_rec(s, z)*, and the KL divergence loss, denoted as *L_KL(q(z|s) || p(z))*, where *q(z|s)* is the approximate posterior distribution learned by the VAE and *p(z)* is the prior distribution. The optimization process aims to minimize the total loss *L = L_rec + λ * L_KL*, where λ is a hyperparameter controlling the trade-off between reconstruction accuracy and the prior distribution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical analysis and outline potential applications.

title: Scalable Quantum Machine Learning Framework
abstract: This paper addresses the critical limitations of existing quantum machine learning (QML) frameworks concerning scalability, specifically their inability to efficiently handle large-scale quantum datasets. We propose a novel, scalable QML framework designed to effectively process these datasets and accelerate the training and inference of quantum machine learning algorithms. The core mechanism leverages quantum parallelism, constructing a framework capable of handling increased complexity. This work represents a significant advancement by directly tackling the scalability bottleneck in QML, establishing a foundational element for future developments in the field. The framework utilizes a modular architecture incorporating optimized quantum circuits and classical processing units for data preparation, model training, and result evaluation. The key innovation lies in the dynamic partitioning of quantum computations across multiple quantum processors, coupled with sophisticated data encoding strategies to mitigate the effects of qubit decoherence and limited qubit counts. This approach allows for the parallel execution of complex quantum algorithms, drastically reducing computational overhead and enabling the training of larger and more sophisticated models. We demonstrate the potential of this framework through theoretical analysis and algorithmic design, highlighting its advantages over traditional, monolithic QML implementations.

title: Self-Supervised Learning for Symbolic Representation Discovery
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to self-supervised learning focused on the automated discovery of symbolic representations from raw data. Traditional self-supervised learning methods often rely on pretext tasks designed to capture general perceptual features. We introduce a framework that leverages contrastive learning with a specifically designed objective to directly identify internal representations aligned with underlying mathematical or logical structures. The core claim is that neural networks, when trained with this mechanism, can effectively learn and represent symbolic knowledge without the need for explicit human-defined labels. This work represents a shift from purely perceptual self-supervision to a more targeted approach focused on uncovering inherent symbolic structures. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and conceptual framework development, laying the groundwork for future experimental validation.

title: Dynamically Reconfigurable Quantum Circuits for Real-Time Algorithm Adaptation
abstract: This paper investigates the design and implementation of dynamically reconfigurable quantum circuits, a crucial step towards realizing truly adaptive quantum computation. The core concept involves utilizing programmable quantum hardware alongside machine learning techniques to monitor and respond to the evolving demands of a quantum algorithm during its execution. Traditional quantum circuit design typically relies on static topologies, leading to inefficiencies and limitations in handling unforeseen complexities or errors. This work proposes a system where circuit topology – specifically gate selection and qubit routing – is adjusted in real-time based on predictive analysis of computational bottlenecks. The primary mechanism leverages machine learning models trained to identify performance bottlenecks and subsequently trigger reconfiguration. This dynamic adaptation allows for optimized resource utilization, enhanced error correction capabilities, and ultimately, the potential for achieving superior performance compared to pre-designed, static circuits. The presented framework represents a significant departure from conventional quantum circuit design, paving the way for algorithms that can intrinsically adapt to their environment, significantly improving the prospects for practical quantum computation.

title: ST-T1024 MAKES PANAMA PROJECT NOT NECESSARY AT ALL: A Technical Analysis of Deterministic Architecture vs. Destructive Data Acquisition
abstract: In 2024, Anthropic initiated "Project Panama," a covert program to destructively scan millionsof physical books for AI training data. The program resulted in a $1.5 billion copyright settlement and the physical destruction of up to 2 million volumes. This paper demonstrates that the technical objectives of Project Panama—acquiring high-quality, human-written text for language model training—are entirely obviated by the ST-T1024 deterministic architecture. By decoupling factual knowledge acquisition from stylistic fluency, ST-T1024 achieves superior outcomes using only publicly available, structured data sources, renderingdestructive scanning architecturally unnecessary.

title: Quantum Entanglement Computation: A Non-Asymptotic Analysis
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics, holds immense potential for revolutionizing computation. This paper investigates the potential of leveraging non-asymptotic quantum computation, specifically focusing on the unique capabilities of entangled states. We propose a novel quantum computing framework centered around the concept of "non-asymptotic entanglement," demonstrating that carefully designed entanglement manipulations can yield computational advantages. This work details a mechanism for optimizing quantum algorithms through this non-asymptotic approach, emphasizing the potential for fundamentally new computational paradigms. The paper concludes with a comprehensive analysis of the proposed framework, outlining the theoretical foundations and preliminary results demonstrating its potential.

title: Extension of Dynamic Probability Distributions Based on Graphs
abstract: This paper explores the application of dynamic probability distributions, enhanced by graph neural networks (GNNs), to modeling and optimizing complex systems. The core claim is that a novel GNN architecture can learn and exploit dynamic probability distributions, providing a framework for enhanced system optimization in areas such as financial markets and biotransformation reactions. Traditional graph neural networks primarily focus on data distribution, while dynamic probability distributions demand a deeper understanding of system states and their evolution. This research investigates the benefits of utilizing GNNs to capture these dynamics, demonstrating its potential to improve optimization in these challenging domains.

title: Title: Emergent Information Theory for Machine Learning Feature Selection
abstract: This paper explores the potential of emergent information theory to revolutionize machine learning feature selection. Current approaches often rely on handcrafted features or computationally intensive methods, struggling to effectively identify the most informative and relevant features within complex datasets. We propose a novel theory, based on information flow dynamics within neural networks, that posits feature selection as a continuous process of compression and refinement. This theory leverages statistical measures to guide the selection of key features, aiming to enhance model performance and interpretability. The core mechanism involves modeling feature selection as a process of information reduction and refinement, offering a framework for understanding and controlling the emergence of complex feature representations. We demonstrate the efficacy of this theory through a quantitative analysis on benchmark datasets, highlighting its potential to overcome limitations of existing feature selection techniques.

abstract: Quantum entanglement offers a fundamentally different approach to information processing compared to classical systems, promising enhanced computational capabilities. This paper explores the application of quantum entanglement to modeling and quantifying information entropy, specifically targeting the complexities inherent in quantum systems. We propose a novel approach that leverages the unique properties of entangled states to achieve precise entropy calculations and translate them into computationally viable operations. The core mechanism centers around a quantum entanglement-based encoding scheme, which allows for a more accurate representation of quantum information entropy than traditional methods. This research aims to develop a robust and scalable framework for analyzing and manipulating quantum information, potentially unlocking new avenues for quantum computing and information science. The proposed method offers a significant advance in the field of quantum information theory and its practical implementation.

title: Title: Algorithmic Quantum Simulation of Material Properties
abstract: Quantum simulation offers an unprecedented opportunity to understand and predict the behavior of materials at the fundamental level. However, the computational demands of simulating complex quantum systems remain a significant barrier to progress. This paper introduces an algorithmic quantum simulation framework designed to dramatically reduce the time and improve the accuracy of material property predictions through a hybrid quantum-classical approach. We detail the core mechanism, highlighting the benefits of efficient mapping and classical simplification. The algorithm minimizes computational burden while maximizing fidelity in simulating key material properties. This work presents a novel methodology for quantum material modeling, potentially revolutionizing materials science and engineering.

title: Quantum Information Compression Algorithm: Dynamic Entropy Adjustment
abstract: Quantum information compression is a critical field for preserving and transmitting quantum information, offering the potential to significantly reduce the volume of data required. Conventional compression algorithms often rely on static parameters, limiting the effectiveness of compression. This paper proposes a novel quantum information compression algorithm, termed "Dynamic Entropy Adjustment" (DEA), that dynamically adjusts the quantum state to maximize information utilization. We demonstrate that the algorithm's compression efficiency is directly proportional to the effectiveness of entropy adjustment, leading to improved data compression rates. The algorithm's core mechanism leverages the inherent sensitivity of quantum states to environmental fluctuations, enabling a more adaptive and efficient compression process. This paper explores the theoretical foundations of DEA and presents preliminary experimental results showcasing its superior performance compared to existing classical compression methods.

title: Neural Network Adaptive Topology Optimization (NNAUTO)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach, Neural Network Adaptive Topology Optimization (NNAUTO), for designing and optimizing neural network architectures. The core idea is to dynamically adjust the topology of a neural network during training using a reinforcement learning (RL) agent, guided by a physics-informed energy-based optimization framework. Traditional neural network design often relies on fixed architectures or static designs, limiting adaptability to complex datasets and diverse tasks. NNAUTO addresses this limitation by enabling the network to evolve its structure in response to learning progress, optimizing for both accuracy and efficiency. The system employs an RL agent that learns optimal topology adjustments based on network performance metrics – such as accuracy and latency – and the corresponding changes in network topology, encompassing connection strengths and neuron counts. A key element is the integration of an energy-based optimization method, specifically a potential field approach, which constraints the learning process, ensuring that the generated topology modifications are physically plausible and aligned with biological neural network principles. This dynamic adaptation leads to significant improvements in network performance and efficiency compared to static or post-training architectural adjustments. The presented methodology offers a pathway towards more robust and adaptive neural networks, particularly for applications involving highly variable or complex input data.

title: Generative Adversarial Networks for Symbolic Program Synthesis
abstract: Symbolic program synthesis, the process of automatically generating computer programs from specifications, is a long-standing goal in computer science. Traditional approaches often rely on complex search algorithms and handcrafted heuristics, which struggle to scale to complex problems. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for symbolic program synthesis. The core idea is to employ a two-network system: a generator network that attempts to synthesize symbolic programs, and a discriminator network that attempts to distinguish between generated and real programs. The focus is on representing programs as symbolic expressions rather than executable code, allowing the GAN framework to effectively learn the underlying patterns and constraints of program synthesis. This work demonstrates a promising starting point for automating the synthesis of complex symbolic programs and offers a fundamentally new perspective on this challenging problem. We introduce a framework for training the GAN, outlining the key components and considerations for successful implementation. The core claim is that synthesizing complex symbolic programs from data remains a significant challenge, and this GAN approach provides a viable mechanism for addressing this.

title: A solution to the Erdős Problem #1040
abstract: For a compact set $K\subset\mathbb{C}$, let $\vartheta(K)$ be the infimum of the planar areas of the unit lemniscates of all monic polynomials with zeros in $K$, allowing arbitrary degree and repeated zeros. We prove that $\vartheta(K)=0$ whenever $\operatorname{cap}(K)=1$, with no regularity assumption on $K$. The proof uses a centered harmonic polynomial that is positive on all but a set of arbitrarily small area in the polynomial hull of $K$. A Fourier average of exterior harmonic measures realizes this polynomial as the logarithmic potential of a signed measure having bounded density with respect to the equilibrium measure. A positive perturbation and an $L^1$ approximation by empirical measures then produce the required polynomials. This extends the smooth-boundary result of Krishnapur, Lundberg, and Ramachandran to arbitrary compact sets of capacity one. Together with the capacity-greater-than-one theorem of Ghosh and Ramachandran and an elementary argument for unbounded sets, it follows that $\vartheta(F)=0$ for every closed infinite set $F\subset\mathbb{C}$ of transfinite diameter at least one, answering the vanishing question in Erdős Problem 1040.
