title: Distilling Vision-Language Models for On-Device Fire Understanding
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising alternative to conventional fire detection systems by reasoning about the semantic context of a scene and thus reducing false alarms, yet their large model size makes deployment on embedded fire sensors impractical. In this paper, we study how domain-specialized VLMs can be compressed for fully on-device deployment without losing the safety-critical behavior required for fire detection. We develop a teacher-student knowledge distillation framework in which large VLMs fine-tuned for fire understanding can be distilled into lightweight students. Experiments across multiple VLM families and model scales show that compact students preserve most of their teachers' fire-understanding capability. We further deploy the distilled models on our commercial Detectium fire detection sensor and jointly evaluate reasoning accuracy, latency, and memory usage. The results show that compression and deployment affect not only accuracy but also model failure modes, with Qwen2.5-0.5B providing the strongest overall deployment trade-off. Our findings provide broader guidance for deploying domain-specialized VLMs in resource-constrained, safety-critical settings.

title: Quantum Mathematics and the P vs NP Problem （量子数学与P vs NP问题）
abstract: Abstract: The P vs NP problem is the central open question in computational complexity theory, asking whether every problem whose solution can be verified in polynomial time can also be solved in polynomial time. This paper argues within the framework of quantum mathematics that P ≠ NP. Quantum mathematics reinterprets natural numbers as quantum states in ℓ2(ℕ), introducing the generation operator 𝐺̂ and the cognition operator 𝐶̂, whose non-commutation relation [𝐺̂,𝐶̂] = 𝑖𝑔𝐼̂ (with 𝑔 = 1/2) constitutes the fundamental dynamics of arithmetic. This paper proves that the solution space for problem instance 𝑛 corresponds to the representation space ℛ(𝑛), whose cardinality ∣ ℛ(𝑛) ∣∼ 𝑒𝑐√𝑛 grows exponentially; the polynomial-step projection of the cognition operator 𝐶̂ can only cover a zero-measure subset of ℛ(𝑛). The proof depends on the four fundamental theorems of quantum mathematics—the non-commutation theorem, the arithmetical uncertainty principle, the prime emergence theorem, and the order conservation theorem—all of which are necessary consequences of the same primordial axiom 𝐺𝐶 = 𝑖𝐶𝐺. This paper reveals that the non-commutation between the generation pole and the cognition pole determines a fundamental structural gap between "solving" (generation) and "verifying" (cognition).摘要：P vs NP 问题是计算复杂性理论的核心未解难题，它询问：所有可在多项式时间 内验证的问题是否也可在多项式时间内求解？本文在量子数学框架内论证P ≠ NP。量 子数学将自然数重新解释为 ℓ2(ℕ) 中的量子态，引入生成算子 𝐺̂ 与认知算子 𝐶̂，其非 对易关系 [𝐺̂,𝐶̂] = 𝑖𝑔𝐼̂（𝑔 = 1/2）构成算术的根本动力学。本文证明：问题实例 𝑛 的 可能解空间对应于表示空间 ℛ(𝑛)，其基数 ∣ℛ(𝑛)∣∼𝑒𝑐√𝑛 指数增长；认知算符 𝐶̂ 的多 项式步数投影只能覆盖 ℛ(𝑛) 的零测度子集。证明依赖于量子数学四个基本定理——非 对易性定理、算术测不准原理、素数涌现定理与秩序守恒定理——它们都是同一原初 公理 𝐺𝐶=𝑖𝐶𝐺 的必然推论。本文揭示：生成极与认知极的非对易性决定了"求解"（生 成）与"验证"（认知）之间存在根本性的结构性鸿沟。

title: Elemental Strategy: Intelligent Board Game
abstract: Video games have evolved from simple entertainment applications into interactive systems that can improve problem-solving, decision-making, and strategic thinking. Artificial Intelligence (AI) plays an important role in modern games through techniques such as pathfinding, decision-making, finite state machines, and dynamic difficulty adjustment. This project presents a 2D grid-based escape game in which the player controls a character that must move from a starting position to an escape door while overcoming different obstacles such as ice, fire, water, and walls. The player is required to make strategic decisions and use appropriate elements, such as fire to melt ice and water to overcome fire-based obstacles, to progress through the game. Pathfinding techniques such as A* and Dijkstra can be used to determine efficient routes while considering obstacles and game conditions. Finite State Machines can also be applied to control intelligent game objects or enemies, while Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment can be used to increase the challenge according to the player's performance. Sound effects provide additional feedback and improve player interaction and engagement. The proposed game combines grid-based movement, obstacle solving, elemental interactions, pathfinding, decision-making, and audio feedback to create an interactive and challenging 2D escape game.

title: Code for: A statistical framework for identifying subgroup vulnerability to predictive multiplicity in clinical AI
abstract: A statistically grounded vulnerability index, V(S), for auditing prespecified patient subgroups for vulnerability to predictive multiplicity between clinical prediction models. V(S) combines an observable lower-bound witness of model disagreement with clinical severity and provides asymptotic inference, a composite intersection-union decision rule, and multiplicity-adjusted testing across subgroups. Applied to in-hospital mortality prediction using a random forest and logistic regression trained on MIMIC-IV (n=65,078) and externally evaluated on eICU-CRD (n=188,230; 208 hospitals) across 158 prespecified subgroups, with four simulation studies characterizing finite-sample operating characteristics of the proposed inference procedures.

title: Quantum Error Correction Encoding and Adaptive Quantum Channel Mapping (QECM)
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to quantum error correction (QEC) and adaptive quantum channel mapping (QECM) designed to enhance the robustness of quantum information transmission through noisy channels. The core idea is to leverage the redundancy inherent in QEC codes and combine it with a machine learning-based adaptive mapping algorithm. Unlike traditional methods that rely on pre-characterized channel models, this approach dynamically optimizes the QEC encoding and channel mapping strategies based on real-time channel feedback. The system utilizes an error correction matrix derived from the chosen QEC code to construct a quantum channel model. A neural network, specifically a variational quantum neural network (VQNN), is then trained to learn the optimal quantum channel mapping policy. This dynamic optimization addresses the limitations of fixed channel models and promises improved performance in practical quantum communication scenarios. The effectiveness of the QECM framework is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and a conceptual model, paving the way for robust long-distance quantum communication. The system's adaptability allows it to cope with unknown or time-varying channel characteristics, a critical factor for successful quantum communication implementations. The ultimate goal is to achieve efficient and reliable quantum information transfer, regardless of the underlying channel noise.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Dynamic Knowledge Graph Evolution
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for constructing and evolving a neuro-symbolic knowledge graph (NSKG) capable of adapting to dynamic changes in information. The core idea is to combine the strengths of deep learning and knowledge graphs, leveraging graph neural networks (GNNs) to learn relationships within the graph and incorporating a reward mechanism to guide optimization towards higher graph quality. Furthermore, the system dynamically integrates knowledge from external sources, allowing for incremental updates and corrections. The resulting NSKG can autonomously learn and evolve, addressing the limitations of static knowledge graphs commonly used in intelligent applications. The key contributions lie in the automated adaptation process and the ability to represent and reason with evolving knowledge. We present a formal model of the system and outline the key components, focusing on the learning process and the dynamic evolution strategy. The system's performance is assessed through a simulated environment, demonstrating its ability to maintain knowledge consistency and accuracy as new information emerges. The overall goal is to create a robust and intelligent knowledge representation system suitable for real-world applications requiring dynamic reasoning.

title: 基于量子自适应的概率模型优化
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum self-adaptive probability model optimization algorithm. Traditional probabilistic models often rely on manual parameter adjustment, limiting the algorithm's effectiveness. This work leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement and quantum computing to achieve a more robust and adaptable optimization process. We propose a quantum-enhanced optimization strategy that dynamically adjusts the model parameters based on quantum correlations, resulting in improved model reliability and generalization capabilities. The algorithm's core mechanism centers around establishing and manipulating quantum entanglement between model parameters, facilitating a more efficient and precise parameter search. This approach offers a promising alternative to classical optimization methods, particularly for complex probabilistic models requiring high accuracy and robustness. The results demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through a series of simulations and comparisons with established optimization techniques, showcasing its potential for significant advancements in probabilistic modeling.

title: Nonlinear Geometric Information Theory
abstract: This paper introduces a novel information theory framework centered around non-linear geometric information, aiming to address limitations of traditional approaches. We propose a dynamic model that leverages geometric information to refine probability predictions, offering a new perspective on data compression and analysis. The core claim is that this approach allows for more accurate modeling of complex geometric distributions, and provides a novel framework for enhanced prediction. The paper details the construction of a probabilistic model that incorporates geometric information, and explores the potential benefits of dynamic geometric structure.

title: Geometry Topology and Quantum Machine Learning
abstract: This paper explores the synergistic potential of geometry topology and quantum machine learning, investigating the possibility of leveraging quantum machine learning to enhance the efficiency and precision of machine learning algorithms. The core claim posits that integrating geometric topology, a field of mathematics concerned with shapes and spaces, with quantum machine learning offers a novel approach to improve computational efficiency and algorithmic accuracy. This research will examine the connection between these two disciplines, focusing on how quantum mechanics can be utilized to optimize data processing and model training. We will delve into the potential benefits of this combination, analyzing specific algorithms and datasets to demonstrate a pathway toward more robust and effective machine learning systems. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and potential applications.

title: Adaptive Topological Quantum Computation
abstract: This paper introduces an innovative quantum computing architecture based on adaptive topological quantum computation. Traditional quantum computing faces challenges related to qubit decoherence and limited scalability. We propose a novel design that leverages the inherent topological properties of qubits to dynamically adjust their arrangement and state, enabling highly efficient quantum algorithms and computations. This architecture overcomes limitations by optimizing quantum states for specific operations, reducing the need for complex gate sequences and enhancing computational speed. The core mechanism centers around the creation of a self-correcting quantum bit array, allowing for continuous adaptation to the task at hand. The potential benefits of this approach include increased computational throughput, reduced error rates, and the ability to implement novel quantum algorithms. This work presents a fundamental shift in design principles for quantum computation, holding the promise of dramatically accelerating quantum processing.

The core mechanism centers around the creation of a self-correcting quantum bit array, allowing for continuous adaptation to the task at hand. The potential benefits of this approach include increased computational throughput, reduced error rates, and the ability to implement novel quantum algorithms. This work presents a fundamental shift in design principles for quantum computation, holding the promise of dramatically accelerating quantum processing.

title: Quantum Topology Information Theory
abstract: Quantum Topology Information Theory explores the profound intersection of quantum mechanics and information theory, proposing a novel framework to leverage the unique properties of quantum topology for enhanced information security. The core claim centers on establishing a quantum topology information theory, investigating its application in information encoding and decryption, and utilizing topological characteristics to bolster security. This research aims to design quantum information algorithms that exploit the inherent robustness and complexity of quantum topology. The study will examine how the topological structure of quantum systems can be harnessed to create more secure and efficient data transmission and storage methods.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Quantum State Generation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to quantum state generation, incorporating a dynamically adaptive mechanism that adjusts the generation process based on input data and environmental conditions. Traditional quantum state generation relies on predefined rules, this design aims to enhance quantum information processing efficiency through dynamic adjustment. The core mechanism involves an adaptive quantum state generator, enabling the system to optimize state creation based on real-time analysis of the input and surrounding environment. This optimization is achieved by a feedback loop that continuously assesses and modifies the state generation parameters, leading to improved performance. The resulting system demonstrates significant improvements in key performance metrics, validating the proposed dynamic adaptation strategy.

title: Adaptive Topology in Neural Networks
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of adaptive topology in neural networks to enhance representation learning and robustness. Traditional neural network architectures are typically fixed, limiting their ability to capture complex patterns. We propose a novel method leveraging reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust network topology – specifically, the connections between neurons – based on the training data. This approach aims to create a system capable of continuously refining network representations, leading to improved performance across a variety of tasks. The core mechanism centers around an iterative refinement process guided by a reinforcement learning agent, optimizing for both accuracy and stability. We explore the benefits of this dynamic adaptation and present preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness in a simulated learning scenario. The focus is on achieving a more flexible and adaptable system than current static approaches.

title: Quantum-Driven Constraint Satisfaction with Adaptive Relaxation
abstract: Quantum-driven constraint satisfaction is an emerging field that leverages quantum mechanics to solve complex optimization problems, particularly those involving constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a novel approach to this problem, employing a quantum annealing algorithm coupled with an adaptive relaxation scheme. We demonstrate that by dynamically adjusting the relaxation criteria during the quantum annealing process, the algorithm significantly improves solution quality compared to traditional methods. The core mechanism centers around a quantum-enhanced exploration of the solution space, guided by a feedback loop that adapts to the system's state. This adaptive relaxation strategy promises to address key limitations of existing constraint satisfaction techniques, offering the potential for enhanced performance and robustness.

title: Adaptive Evolutionary Program Synthesis for Semantic Understanding
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to program synthesis that leverages the principles of evolutionary computation. The core idea is to treat program synthesis as an optimization problem, where a population of programs is iteratively evolved based on their ability to satisfy a given semantic description. We introduce a framework where genetic algorithms are employed to modify program structures and parameters, driven by feedback from the target semantics. Unlike conventional program synthesis techniques that rely heavily on predefined rules and templates, our approach promotes adaptive learning and self-optimization, leading to programs that are more robust and tailored to the specific requirements. The primary goal is to achieve a deeper understanding of the semantic intent behind the desired program, translating natural language or other high-level specifications into executable code. We explore the effectiveness of this methodology through a conceptual framework, outlining the key components and potential challenges. This work lays the foundation for a new paradigm in program synthesis – one that embraces the power of evolution for truly intelligent code generation.

title: Adaptive Differential Privacy via Dynamic Thresholds
abstract: This paper introduces a novel adaptive differential privacy (DP) mechanism designed to mitigate the limitations of traditional DP approaches, particularly concerning excessive noise addition in scenarios with small datasets. The core idea is to dynamically adjust the noise scale based on the sensitivity of the query and the current state of the data. This is achieved through the integration of a reinforcement learning (RL) agent that learns optimal thresholds for noise addition. The RL agent's objective is to minimize privacy loss while simultaneously preserving data utility. We demonstrate that this dynamic thresholding approach offers a significantly improved trade-off between privacy and utility compared to fixed noise scales commonly employed in DP. The theoretical analysis provides insights into the convergence properties of the RL agent and the overall privacy guarantees offered by the mechanism. The proposed method represents a crucial step towards more efficient and effective DP implementations, particularly in resource-constrained settings where minimizing noise is paramount.

title: Non-Linear Geometry for Quantum Entanglement Simulation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum entanglement simulation method based on non-linear geometry, aiming to significantly enhance the accuracy of capturing the complex non-linear properties of quantum entanglement. We propose a framework that leverages geometric structures to simulate entanglement states, employing self-adaptive geometric transformations to effectively model the system's inherent non-linearity. The core mechanism centers around constructing a geometric representation of the entangled state that allows for more precise and robust simulation of this crucial phenomenon. This approach offers a potential pathway to more powerful and reliable quantum computation, surpassing the limitations of traditional methods. The paper details the design of the geometric structure, the implementation of the self-adaptive transformations, and preliminary results demonstrating improved entanglement fidelity compared to existing classical approaches. We conclude with a discussion of the implications of this method for the future of quantum computing.

title: Dense Interprocedural Dominance in Acyclic Graphs: Context Bounds and Compact Queries
abstract: Interprocedural dominance asks which program points every matched call-and-return execution must pass on its way to a target. An analysis that writes out immediate dominance pays for the transitive reduction of this order, the minimal dominator graph. Measured instances of that graph look near-linear, with edge-to-node ratios around 1.1--1.26~\cite{DeSutter2007}, but no program property is known to force this: it is unclear which structural restrictions imply sparse output, and whether dense output also rules out cheap queries. This paper answers both through calling contexts. A static node stands for the group of its reachable configurations; write $κ$ for the largest group size and $α$ for how many nodes have more than one configuration. One context per node keeps the tree with $n-1$ edges. Two already allow $Θ(n^2)$ cover edges in a sparse, loop-free, recursion-free ICFG with total degree three, constant-size procedures, and logarithmic stack depth, while the reachable configuration graph itself stays linear, so the blowup comes from grouping, not from many configurations. Three keep $Θ(n^2)$ covers even when the explicit call/return graph is acyclic: all target-reaching runs visit the mandatory procedures in the same order, and extra runs that stop short of any target remove the comparabilities that would otherwise kill the covers. Complementing the lower bounds, $α$ ambiguous nodes admit at most $\min\{\floor{n^2/4},(α+1)(n-1)\}$ cover edges, with $Ω(αn)$ attainable at stack depth one. And for every ICFG with at most two contexts per node, deleting a context group reduces dominance to dual-failure reachability, giving $O(n)$-word, $O(1)$-query representation after polynomial preprocessing. Explicit cover size, context ambiguity, and query-space cost are three separate quantities.

title: Preference-Shift Diagnostics for Iterative Policy Refinement
abstract: The deployment of autonomous systems in dynamic, human-centric environments necessitates continuous adaptation to evolving user preferences. Iterative policy refinement, a cornerstone of modern reinforcement learning and alignment strategies, often assumes stationary preference distributions. However, human preferences are inherently non-stationary, exhibiting complex temporal, contextual, and systemic shifts that degrade policy performance over time. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework for preference-shift diagnostics designed to identify, categorize, and address non-stationarity in iterative policy refinement pipelines. By establishing a robust diagnostic methodology, this research bridges the gap between static reward modeling and dynamic operational environments. We propose a multi-layered diagnostic architecture that continuously monitors feedback streams, detects distributional divergences, and attributes these shifts to specific environmental or human factors. Through extensive theoretical analysis and simulated experimental validation, we demonstrate that integrating preference-shift diagnostics significantly enhances the resilience and alignment of autonomous policies. The findings underscore the critical need for diagnostic transparency in policy optimization, providing a scalable solution for maintaining system efficacy in the face of shifting human expectations.

title: ENGRAFT: ENgram GRadient Routing-Aware Fact Transplant
abstract: First public release of ENGRAFT (ENgram GRadient Routing-Aware Fact Transplant): add a fact to Qwen3.8-Flash-Next by gradient descent on the 8 trigram-keyed rows of its n-gram (Engram/PLE) table, through a CPU replica of the frozen model with expert routing refreshed at every step, shipped as an overlay the engine substitutes at read time. What is in this release: the code (Apache 2.0), an offline quick start against fakes, and scripts/reproduce.sh for the real model; the run of record results/2026-09-05/: 7 of 8 facts reproduced by the real llama.cpp engine at first-token probability 0.85 to 0.96, merged overlay identical to single overlays, sister triggers unchanged, CPU replica equal to the full-precision engine on 17 of 17 grafts; the technical report paper/engraft.pdf (CC BY 4.0), attached below. Limitations are stated in the README and in the report: the grafts do not generalize to the fact stated inside a document, one counterfactual fact with a concentrated base-model prior does not take, one model and one run of eight facts. How this was built: the code, the experiments and the write-up were produced in a Claude Code session (Anthropic's Claude, model Fable 5.1) driven by a single human operator who set the goals, approved every design step, ran the hardware and read every result. We want the method checked, broken and improved.

title: Quantum Machine Learning with Multi-Variable Entangled Encoding
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of multi-variable entangled encoding as a novel approach to enhance quantum machine learning algorithms. The core claim is that exploiting multi-variable entanglement can significantly improve the parallel computation capabilities and information storage efficiency within these algorithms. The proposed mechanism involves encoding multiple quantum bits into multi-variable entangled states. Leveraging the inherent correlations within these entangled states allows for parallel computations and information compression. We explore theoretical frameworks and mathematical formulations to demonstrate the feasibility and potential advantages of this technique. The research provides a new perspective on optimizing quantum machine learning algorithms, addressing limitations in current approaches and paving the way for more efficient quantum data processing. This work focuses on the fundamental principles and theoretical underpinnings, without requiring experimental validation.

title: Hierarchical Abstraction Learning for Large-Scale Data
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for hierarchical abstraction learning designed to efficiently process and understand large-scale datasets. The core idea is to automate the discovery of hierarchical representations, which drastically reduces the complexity of data analysis. We introduce a recursive clustering algorithm guided by information-theoretic measures, specifically mutual information, to iteratively refine data representations and construct a hierarchy of abstractions. This approach addresses a significant challenge in dealing with massive datasets by providing a scalable and automated method for identifying underlying patterns and structure. The resulting hierarchical structure facilitates intuitive data exploration and understanding, potentially leading to improved insights and decision-making. We demonstrate the framework's efficacy through theoretical analysis and outline potential applications across diverse domains.

title: Representation Alignment Compass Core Semantic Package: A Stable Machine-Readable Contract for Alignment Research and System Design
abstract: Representation alignment research now spans multimodal, cross-lingual, cross-domain, multi-view, and model-to-model systems, with a rapidly expanding range of models, losses, matching procedures, and training strategies. However, the design decisions that determine whether an alignment strategy is appropriate for a particular problem are often implicit in technical choices or scattered across papers, code, experiments, and local discussion. A method name and its reported performance may show what was used and how it performed without making clear what compatibility was intended, what correspondence was assumed, what information should remain distinct, or why those choices fit the problem. This makes it harder to design systems around the requirements of the problem, compare methods at a common design level, and carry design intent reliably into implementation. Existing resources support important parts of this work. Surveys and taxonomies help researchers understand which alignment methods and research families have been developed. Experiment platforms record what was run and how it performed, while provenance and documentation standards capture where artifacts came from, how they were produced, and how they are intended to be used. These resources make methods, experiments, and artifacts easier to find, reproduce, and inspect. The design rationale connecting a particular problem to a particular form of alignment, however, can remain embedded in local terminology, technical choices, and project-specific documentation. As a result, knowledge generated through earlier design work can remain difficult to compare across projects, transfer between teams, or accumulate into a reusable body of knowledge. The Representation Alignment Compass (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22096467) provides a compact and relatively stable design-level reference for the high-leverage commitments that determine what form of alignment a problem requires. The Representation Alignment Compass Core Semantic Package (RAC-CORE) makes this reference machine-readable and persistent, allowing alignment commitments, context, evidence, intended designs, executed configurations, and evaluation artifacts to remain connected through a shared semantic structure as methods and implementations evolve. This provides a common basis for explicit design, coherent interpretation of a changing field, cumulative evidence across projects, and shared reasoning across researchers, teams, tools, and computational agents. Theoretical Framework, Core Package, and Practical Companion RAC-CORE is the machine-readable component of a broader three-resource Representation Alignment architecture. This Zenodo record contains RAC-CORE only; the Theoretical Framework and Practical Companion are separate resources. The framework defines the conceptual design semantics, RAC-CORE preserves those semantics in machine-readable records, and the Practical Companion supports their practical application. Theoretical Framework. Use the published Representation Alignment Compass when the primary need is to understand representation alignment, compare design alternatives, or reason about the high-leverage commitments that should shape a research or system-design problem. It remains authoritative for the conceptual architecture, category meanings, and design logic. Core Semantic Package. Use RAC-CORE when those commitments need to become persistent machine-readable records that can be reviewed, exchanged, versioned, linked to evidence or execution, or reused across projects and computational workflows. RAC-CORE is authoritative for machine-readable semantics and conformance. Practical Companion. The Practical Companion, when released separately on GitHub, will provide richer worked examples, guided authoring, templates, workbenches, integration utilities, and other practice-facing support. It will remain pinned to an exact RAC-CORE release while leaving the conceptual framework and Core semantics unchanged. Core Values 1. Making Alignment Designs Explicit and Reviewable RAC-CORE turns the high-leverage commitments identified through the theoretical framework into an explicit, context-scoped design record. Problem conditions, selected configurations, unresolved choices, rationale, and proposed technical realizations can be examined together rather than reconstructed from separate artifacts. Researchers and system designers can use this record to evaluate whether a design is coherent with its intended purpose and constraints, compare candidate configurations, revise specific commitments, and carry the design reliably into implementation or handoff. The theoretical framework supports the reasoning; RAC-CORE preserves the resulting design state in a form that can be reviewed, versioned, and continued. 2. Maintaining a Coherent and Evolvable Alignment Knowledge Structure Alignment methods, models, losses, and implementations can change rapidly while the higher-level design commitments they realize remain comparatively stable. RAC-CORE allows these technical objects to remain externally versioned while linking them to a persistent alignment architecture. New work can therefore be incorporated into an existing body of knowledge rather than creating another isolated technical category, and users can compare contributions at the level of alignment design rather than method name alone. The structure remains stable where its design distinctions continue to hold, while recurring evidence of genuinely new alignment logic can motivate a governed Core revision. This provides a stable basis for building a coherent and evolvable knowledge structure across alignment work. 3. Building an Evidence Base for Cumulative Learning and Long-Horizon Planning Learning across projects requires more than preserving individual results; experiences must be expressed in a form that allows them to be related across changing methods and contexts. RAC-CORE keeps literature interpretations, intended designs, executed configurations, and evaluation evidence distinguishable but linkable under a stable semantic reference. As reviewed and traceable records accumulate, heterogeneous projects can be represented as structured evidence that can later be assessed for comparability, synthesis, and recurring design patterns under separately governed analysis. This evidence can support later synthesis, diagnosis, meta-level learning, and long-horizon planning under separately governed analytical processes. RAC-CORE does not supply the learned conclusions itself; it provides the common reference structure through which past experience can become usable evidence for future reasoning. 4. Preserving Shared Alignment Semantics Across Projects, Teams, and Agents RAC-CORE provides a common semantic contract for alignment work that moves across projects, researchers, teams, software tools, and computational agents. Canonical identities remain tied to their context, scope, evidence, provenance, uncertainty, and governing release, so records can be exchanged without relying on local terminology or undocumented assumptions to recover their meaning. This supports reliable handoff, cross-project synthesis, accountable revision, machine-assisted review, and long-horizon human–agent collaboration while allowing participants to retain their own methods, datasets, and implementation environments. Supported Tasks RAC-CORE supports two peer machine tasks built on the same theoretical coordinates but representing different epistemic objects. RAC-MAP — Represent an Existing Alignment Design from Evidence Use RAC-MAP when an alignment design already exists and must be interpreted from evidence. The evidence may come from a publication or from direct observation of an executed system, according to the channels defined by the released contract. A RAC-MAP record captures the bounded source being interpreted, the relevant context, the alignment commitments and configurations supported by the evidence, provenance, and the limits of permissible inference. It is designed to preserve partial knowledge without forcing unsupported completion. Publication-derived interpretation and execution-grounded observation remain distinguishable, so what a paper claims and what a system actually executes can be recorded separately. Typical uses include literature and method mapping, system inspection, systematic review, evidence-synthesis datasets, design-history reconstruction, and the construction of reusable alignment-design corpora. RAC-DESIGN — Represent an Intended Alignment Design Use RAC-DESIGN when an alignment strategy is being formulated, reviewed, handed off, or revised. A RAC-DESIGN record captures the problem context, intended alignment commitments, candidate configurations, rationale, unresolved choices, and proposed technical realizations. Concrete methods and implementations remain external objects, allowing technical alternatives to change without redefining the Compass. After implementation, the intended design can be linked to an execution-grounded RAC-MAP and to the associated implementation and evaluation evidence. Typical uses include research planning, system-design specification, design review, team or agent handoff, versioned revision, and traceability from an intended alignment route to its realized form. Downstream Comparison and Learning Conformant RAC records provide a common basis for later comparison, aggregation, visualization, and learning. Shared semantic coordinates make it possible to examine recurring commitments and differences across records, while preserved context and epistemic status help determine whether those records are meaningfully comparable. evidence.title: Representation Alignment Compass Core Semantic Package: A Stable Machine-Readable Contract for Alignment Research and System Design
evidence.abstract: Representation alignment research now spans multimodal, cross-lingual, cross-domain, multi-view, and model-to-model systems, with a rapidly expanding range of models, losses, matching procedures, and training strategies. However, the design decisions that determine whether an alignment strategy is appropriate for a particular problem are often implicit in technical choices or scattered across papers, code, experiments, and local discussion. A method name and its reported performance may show what was used and how it performed without making clear what compatibility was intended, what correspondence was assumed, what information should remain distinct, or why those choices fit the problem. This makes it harder to design systems around the requirements of the problem, compare methods at a common design level, and carry design intent reliably into implementation. Existing resources support important parts of this work. Surveys and taxonomies help researchers understand which alignment methods and research families have been developed. Experiment platforms record what was run and how it performed, while provenance and documentation standards capture where artifacts came from, how they were produced, and how they are intended to be used. These resources make methods, experiments, and artifacts easier to find, reproduce, and inspect. The design rationale connecting a particular problem to a particular form of alignment, however, can remain embedded in local terminology, technical choices, and project-specific documentation. As a result, knowledge generated through earlier design work can remain difficult to compare across projects, transfer between teams, or accumulate into a reusable body of knowledge. The Representation Alignment Compass (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22096467) provides a compact and relatively stable design-level reference for the high-leverage commitments that determine what form of alignment a problem requires. The Representation Alignment Compass Core Semantic Package (RAC-CORE) makes this reference machine-readable and persistent, allowing alignment commitments, context, evidence, intended designs, executed configurations, and evaluation artifacts to remain connected through a shared semantic structure as methods and implementations evolve. This provides a common basis for explicit design, coherent interpretation of a changing field, cumulative evidence across projects, and shared reasoning across researchers, teams, tools, and computational agents. Theoretical Framework, Core Package, and Practical Companion RAC-CORE is the machine-readable component of a broader three-resource Representation Alignment architecture. This Zenodo record contains RAC-CORE only; the Theoretical Framework and Practical Companion are separate resources. The framework defines the conceptual design semantics, RAC-CORE preserves those semantics in machine-readable records, and the Practical Companion supports their practical application. Theoretical Framework. Use the published Representation Alignment Compass when the primary need is to understand representation alignment, compare design alternatives, or reason about the high-leverage commitments that should shape a research or system-design problem. It remains authoritative for the conceptual architecture, category meanings, and design logic. Core Semantic Package. Use RAC-CORE when those commitments need to become persistent machine-readable records that can be reviewed, exchanged, versioned, linked to evidence or execution, or reused across projects and computational workflows. RAC-CORE is authoritative for machine-readable semantics and conformance. Practical Companion. The Practical Companion, when released separately on GitHub, will provide richer worked examples, guided authoring, templates, workbenches, integration utilities, and other practice-facing support. It will remain pinned to an exact RAC-CORE release while leaving the conceptual framework and Core semantics unchanged. Core Values 1. Making Alignment Designs Explicit and Reviewable RAC-CORE turns the high-leverage commitments identified through the theoretical framework into an explicit, context-scoped design record. Problem conditions, selected configurations, unresolved choices, rationale, and proposed technical realizations can be examined together rather than reconstructed from separate artifacts. Researchers and system designers can use this record to evaluate whether a design is coherent with its intended purpose and constraints, compare candidate configurations, revise specific commitments, and carry the design reliably into implementation or handoff. The theoretical framework supports the reasoning; RAC-CORE preserves the resulting design state in a form that can be reviewed, versioned, and continued. 2. Maintaining a Coherent and Evolvable Alignment Knowledge Structure Alignment methods, models, losses, and implementations can change rapidly while the higher-level design commitments they realize remain comparatively stable. RAC-CORE allows these technical objects to remain externally versioned while linking them to a persistent alignment architecture. New work can therefore be incorporated into an existing body of knowledge rather than creating another isolated technical category, and users can compare contributions at the level of alignment design rather than method name alone. The structure remains stable where its design distinctions continue to hold, while recurring evidence of genuinely new alignment logic can motivate a governed Core revision. This provides a stable basis for building a coherent and evolvable knowledge structure across alignment work. 3. Building an Evidence Base for Cumulative Learning and Long-Horizon Planning Learning across projects requires more than preserving individual results; experiences must be expressed in a form that allows them to be related across changing methods and contexts. RAC-CORE keeps literature interpretations, intended designs, executed configurations, and evaluation evidence distinguishable but linkable under a stable semantic reference. As reviewed and traceable records accumulate, heterogeneous projects can be represented as structured evidence that can later be assessed for comparability, synthesis, and recurring design patterns under separately governed analysis. This evidence can support later synthesis, diagnosis, meta-level learning, and long-horizon planning under separately governed analytical processes. RAC-CORE does not supply the learned conclusions itself; it provides the common reference structure through which past experience can become usable evidence for future reasoning. 4. Preserving Shared Alignment Semantics Across Projects, Teams, and Agents RAC-CORE provides a common semantic contract for alignment work that moves across projects, researchers, teams, software tools, and computational agents. Canonical identities remain tied to their context, scope, evidence, provenance, uncertainty, and governing release, so records can be exchanged without relying on local terminology or undocumented assumptions to recover their meaning. This supports reliable handoff, cross-project synthesis, accountable revision, machine-assisted review, and long-horizon human–agent collaboration while allowing participants to retain their own methods, datasets, and implementation environments. Supported Tasks RAC-CORE supports two peer machine tasks built on the same theoretical coordinates but representing different epistemic objects. RAC-MAP — Represent an Existing Alignment Design from Evidence Use RAC-MAP when an alignment design already exists and must be interpreted from evidence. The evidence may come from a publication or from direct observation of an executed system, according to the channels defined by the released contract. A RAC-MAP record captures the bounded source being interpreted, the relevant context, the alignment commitments and configurations supported by the evidence, provenance, and the limits of permissible inference. It is designed to preserve partial knowledge without forcing unsupported completion. Publication-derived interpretation and execution-grounded observation remain distinguishable, so what a paper claims and what a system actually executes can be recorded separately. Typical uses include literature and method mapping, system inspection, systematic review, evidence-synthesis datasets, design-history reconstruction, and the construction of reusable alignment-design corpora. RAC-DESIGN — Represent an Intended Alignment Design Use RAC-DESIGN when an alignment strategy is being formulated, reviewed, handed off, or revised. A RAC-DESIGN record captures the problem context, intended alignment commitments, candidate configurations, rationale, unresolved choices, and proposed technical realizations. Concrete methods and implementations remain external objects, allowing technical alternatives to change without redefining the Compass. After implementation, the intended design can be linked to an execution-grounded RAC-MAP and to the associated implementation and evaluation evidence. Typical uses include research planning, system-design specification, design review, team or agent handoff, versioned revision, and traceability from an intended alignment route to its realized form. Downstream Comparison and Learning Conformant RAC records provide a common basis for later comparison, aggregation, visualization, and learning. Shared semantic coordinates make it possible to examine recurring commitments and differences across records, while preserved context and epistemic status help determine whether those records are meaningfully comparable. Any ranking, recommendation, learned tendency, or design-selection procedure remains a downstream analytical responsibility with its own evidence, assumptions, and governance. title: Causal Graph Embedding with Counterfactual Reasoning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph embedding that integrates causal reasoning, specifically leveraging counterfactual analysis. Traditional graph embedding techniques primarily focus on capturing structural relationships within a graph, neglecting the underlying causal dependencies. This limitation hinders the ability to perform "what-if" scenarios or understand the impact of changes on the graph. Our method proposes training a graph embedding model that explicitly learns to represent causal relationships between nodes. This enables the model to answer counterfactual questions, predicting how the graph would evolve under different hypothetical scenarios. We demonstrate the core claim that incorporating causal reasoning significantly enhances graph embeddings, leading to improved counterfactual inference capabilities. The key mechanism involves learning representations that capture directional causal links, allowing the model to effectively simulate changes and predict outcomes. This approach opens up new possibilities for analyzing complex systems represented as graphs, particularly those where causal understanding is crucial for decision-making and prediction.

title: Quantum Resonance Cascade for Algorithmic Complexity
abstract: Quantum Resonance Cascade (QRC) is a novel approach to accelerate the convergence of complex optimization algorithms, particularly evolutionary algorithms, by leveraging quantum entanglement and superposition to dynamically adjust resonance frequencies within a carefully engineered network. This paper presents a detailed theoretical framework and preliminary experimental validation demonstrating the potential of QRC to significantly reduce the computational cost and improve the quality of solutions generated by these algorithms. We explore the fundamental principles of QRC and its application to optimizing complex, multi-variable problems. The core mechanism involves creating a quantum network that resonates at specific frequencies, influencing the evolution of the optimization process. We investigate how this network's structure and the precise application of quantum entanglement can dramatically enhance convergence rates and ensure the exploration of more optimal regions of the solution space. This work offers a fundamentally new perspective on algorithmic optimization and holds promise for accelerating the discovery of advanced solutions across diverse scientific and engineering domains.

title: Title: Adaptive Fractal Dimension - Self-Organizing Data Structures
abstract: This paper presents a novel methodology for automatically generating fractal dimension within data structures, offering a powerful tool for creating highly efficient and adaptable data representations. The core concept revolves around a self-organizing algorithm that iteratively adjusts the fractal dimension based on the inherent structure of the data, ensuring optimal representation for a range of applications. We detail the algorithm's design, its performance evaluation, and a discussion of its potential implications for data science and engineering. The central claim is that this approach facilitates the creation of data structures with dynamically adaptable dimensions, enabling significant improvements in efficiency and flexibility.

title: Probability Logic Networks (PLN) – Adaptive Tensor Representation
abstract: Probability Logic Networks (PLN) represent knowledge as a set of logical rules and probabilities. The effectiveness of a PLN hinges significantly on the quality of its learned representations, particularly the weights associated with each node in the network. This paper explores the development of a novel Adaptive Tensor Representation (ATR) for PLN, aiming to enhance model generalization by dynamically adjusting tensor weights based on input data variations. We introduce a "tensor perception" mechanism, leveraging probabilistic models to evaluate the changes in tensor representations and iteratively refine the network's weights. The proposed approach contrasts with traditional methods by offering a mechanism for self-adaptation, potentially leading to improved performance across diverse datasets. This research presents a framework for dynamically adjusting tensor weights, thereby fostering enhanced generalization capabilities within the PLN.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Emergent System Design
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to designing and simulating emergent systems using probabilistic programming. The core idea is to leverage the inherent ability of probabilistic programming languages to explicitly model uncertainty and explore complex, non-deterministic behaviors. The proposed design space incorporates a domain-specific language (DSL) focused on decentralized systems with partial observability, emphasizing adaptive learning and robust design principles. We argue that this combination represents a significant advancement, providing a powerful tool for tackling the inherent challenges of designing systems where emergent properties arise from complex interactions and incomplete information. The paper outlines the key components of the DSL, detailing its mechanisms for representing system components, defining interactions, and incorporating uncertainty. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a conceptual framework, highlighting its applicability to various emergent system scenarios, without performing actual experiments.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Simulating Complex System Dynamics
abstract: This paper explores the application of probabilistic programming techniques for simulating complex system dynamics, particularly those exhibiting inherent uncertainty. Traditional system simulation often relies on deterministic models built upon simplifying assumptions, which can limit their accuracy and generalizability. This work advocates for the use of probabilistic programming languages—such as Stan and PyMC3—to represent and simulate these systems. These languages allow the construction of Bayesian networks, facilitating the incorporation of prior knowledge, the quantification of uncertainty, and the exploration of a wider range of possible outcomes. The core claim is that probabilistic programming provides a more realistic and robust approach to system simulation by explicitly acknowledging and modeling uncertainty. We demonstrate how this methodology can improve the sensitivity of simulation results to model parameters and provide a more comprehensive understanding of system behavior. The key innovation lies in the seamless integration of statistical modeling and simulation within a single framework, enabling researchers to move beyond purely deterministic approaches.

title: 基于量子神经网络的复杂系统建模
abstract: This paper explores the potential of Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) for modeling and simulating complex systems. Traditional neural networks often struggle with the inherent non-linearity and high dimensionality characteristic of complex systems, leading to inaccuracies and computational challenges. QNNs, leveraging principles of quantum mechanics such as superposition and entanglement, offer a fundamentally different approach that may overcome these limitations. This work outlines a framework for constructing a QNN specifically designed for complex system modeling, detailing the key components and potential advantages. The core claim is that QNNs can provide a more accurate and efficient method for modeling and simulating complex systems. We introduce a novel mechanism utilizing quantum properties for enhanced representation and processing of complex system dynamics. This represents a new approach to complex system modeling, offering the possibility of uncovering previously hidden patterns and behaviors. This document focuses on the theoretical foundation and design principles of this approach, without involving experimental validation.

title: Graph-Based Representation Learning for Natural Language Processing
abstract: This paper explores the application of graph-based representation learning to the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). Traditional NLP models frequently encounter difficulties in effectively capturing the intricate relationships between words, particularly those spanning significant distances within a sentence or document – a phenomenon known as long-range dependency. We propose a novel approach that represents sentences as graphs, utilizing words as nodes and semantic relationships as edges. The core idea is to learn word embeddings directly from this graph structure, enabling the model to inherently capture these long-range dependencies. This method offers a potentially more robust and efficient way to represent textual data compared to traditional methods relying solely on sequential processing, addressing a key limitation in current NLP techniques. We will detail the graph construction process, embedding learning strategies, and present initial insights into the model's performance.

title: Physics-Based Simulation for AI Model Training
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to Artificial Intelligence (AI) model training by leveraging physics-based simulation. Traditional AI training, particularly deep learning, relies heavily on vast datasets and significant computational resources, presenting substantial barriers to entry and scalability. This work proposes a method where the training process of an AI model is mapped and simulated within a physics engine. The engine provides interactive and feedback mechanisms, allowing for the adjustment of model parameters and structure based on physical interactions. We demonstrate the potential of this approach to reduce training costs and resource consumption, offering a fundamentally different paradigm for AI development. The core claim is that utilizing physics engines for AI training avoids the resource intensity of conventional methods. The underlying mechanism involves mapping AI training to a simulated environment, gaining feedback through physical interactions. This new method promises to lower training costs and resource requirements.

title: Adaptive Kernel Learning for Data Representation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to data representation leveraging adaptive kernel learning. Traditional kernel methods, such as Support Vector Machines, rely on fixed kernels, a limitation that restricts their adaptability to diverse data distributions. Our methodology addresses this by dynamically learning the kernel function itself. This is achieved through a recurrent neural network trained on the data's kernel matrix, allowing the kernel to adjust its parameters based on local data density and feature correlations. The core claim is that fixed kernels significantly limit the performance of kernel methods, and the proposed adaptive kernel learning provides a more flexible and accurate representation. The algorithm's key innovation lies in its ability to move beyond static kernel definitions, offering substantial improvements in accuracy across a range of datasets. The theoretical framework is outlined, followed by a discussion of the algorithm's implementation and potential applications. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a conceptual framework and provide a detailed explanation of the underlying mathematical principles.

title: Probabilistic Logical Programming: A Bayesian Inference Framework
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for probabilistic reasoning by integrating probabilistic logic programming with Bayesian inference. The core claim is to establish a new programming paradigm capable of handling uncertainty and probabilistic reasoning problems. This is achieved by combining the symbolic reasoning capabilities of probabilistic logic with the statistical inference capabilities of Bayesian methods. The framework addresses a critical limitation of existing probabilistic logic programming approaches, which predominantly rely on logical deduction without robust mechanisms for managing and reasoning with uncertain knowledge. The proposed system introduces a layered approach, allowing for both explicit logical rules and probabilistic assessments, ultimately leading to more comprehensive and adaptable reasoning systems. This work outlines the key components of the framework and presents a foundational approach for developing intelligent systems that can effectively navigate complex, uncertain environments. The system aims to improve the accuracy and robustness of probabilistic inference, offering a valuable tool for domains such as expert systems, medical diagnosis, and risk assessment.

title: SignDino: Self-Supervised Sign Language Representation Learning via Temporal-Axis Self-Distillation
abstract: Self-supervised sign language representation learning must model two properties not central to natural-image SSL: signs are produced by a small set of anatomically distinct articulators, and their meaning depends on the temporal organisation of those articulators. We introduce SignDino, a self-supervised sign-video encoder that moves the DINOv3 student--teacher recipe from the spatial domain of image crops to the temporal domain of tracked sign streams. Each video is decomposed into left-hand, right-hand, and face streams by a detector-first YOLOv8n+ByteTrack pipeline. A frozen DINOv3 ViT-B/16 embeds each per-frame anatomical crop, while lightweight temporal Transformers, not the image backbone, form the student and EMA teacher. They are trained by temporal DINO self-distillation, frame-level masked-token prediction in the style of iBOT, KoLeo feature spreading, and Gram anchoring of the frame-to-frame similarity structure. This design keeps strong image-level visual primitives fixed and learns only how articulator states evolve across time. We evaluate on sign-to-English translation, isolated sign recognition, and fingerspelling detection benchmarks. Across these tasks, SignDino provides a strong public self-supervised representation and shows competitive or state-of-the-art performance under matched downstream evaluation.

title: Nonlinear elliptic homogenization with the parametric Deep Ritz method
abstract: Elliptic homogenization is used to determine coarse-grained properties of materials with features on small scales. When these small scale features have rapid, periodic fluctuations, the solution field corresponding to a homogenized constitutive relation closely resembles the true solution based on the heterogeneous material. This homogenized behavior of the material is computed from a cell problem, where a cell is defined to be one period of the fluctuating material. In the context of linear elliptic partial differential equations, the homogenized constitutive relation is defined simply by a constant coefficient tensor, but for nonlinear problems, the homogenized response depends on the macroscopic state and/or its gradient, thus requiring solutions to parametric cell problems. When computing a numerical solution with the homogenized constitutive relation, it is useful to have a differentiable representation of the solution to the cell problem, as derivatives of the homogenized constitutive relation are required in Newton iterations for the macroscopic state field. In this work, we use the Deep Ritz method to solve the parametric cell problems that arise from nonlinear homogenization. First, we exploit the variational structure of the cell problem, then we discretize the dependence of the cell response on both space and the macroscopic state with a neural network. Enforcing boundary conditions on the cell response strongly, we next use the parametric Deep Ritz method to simultaneously solve the cell problem over a range of macroscopic states. We show that this method is accurate, efficient, and offers a continuous and differentiable representation of the cell response over the macroscopic state and gradient. We then show that our parametric representation of the cell response significantly expedites macroscale solutions when compared to a traditional $\text{FE}^2$ scheme.

title: Layered Cryptographic Trust for Open Digital Systems: A Conceptual Framework Linking Private-Key Limitations, Public-Key Exchange and Post-Quantum Migration
abstract: Modern digital infrastructures rely on cryptography to establish confidentiality, integrity, authentication, non-repudiation and secure key establishment over networks that cannot be assumed trustworthy. Yet the relationship between private-key limitations, public-key exchange, computational security, pseudorandomness, chosen-plaintext security and post-quantum migration is often presented in fragmented form. This study develops a layered design-science framework for cryptographic trust in open digital systems. The work adopts a conceptual review method supported by standards-based triangulation. Core techniques were analysed against their security role, mathematical basis, computing requirements, application domain, operational risk and post-quantum relevance. The resulting framework shows that symmetric encryption remains the most practical mechanism for high-volume data protection, but it depends on reliable key establishment and lifecycle governance. Public-key cryptography provides scalable trust and authentication, while Diffie-Hellman exchange and key derivation functions connect mathematical shared-secret construction to deployable session keys. Pseudorandomness and chosen-plaintext security give formal discipline to encryption design, whereas post-quantum cryptography introduces migration requirements for long-term confidentiality and identity assurance. The study contributes an integrated architecture that connects cryptographic theory, implementation practice and institutional readiness. Its main implication is that secure systems should be designed as hybrid, lifecycle-aware and algorithm-agile infrastructures rather than as isolated deployments of individual cryptographic primitives.

title: Division and Modulo from Recursive Normalization
abstract: We define integer division and modulo by recursively normalizing quotient–remainder states and verify the construction in Scala Stainless. We prove uniqueness of the normalized solution, compatibility with native modulo for nonnegative dividends and positive divisors, invariance under shifts by multiples of the divisor, together with addition, subtraction, and modulo-idempotence laws. We also verify the unit-step quotient–remainder transition and that every block of p consecutive nonnegative integers, for p > 1, contains exactly one zero remainder modulo p. Together, these results show that recursive normalization is canonical on the stated domains and recovers the verified algebraic and periodic laws of division and modulo.

title: Contextualized Memory Networks with Dynamic Attention
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to Memory Networks (MemNets) designed to address the limitations of existing models in effectively utilizing memory based on context. The core problem lies in the static nature of memory access within standard MemNets, which often leads to inefficient information processing. We propose a Contextualized Memory Network (CMN) incorporating a dynamic attention mechanism. This mechanism allows the network to learn and assign weights to memory slots dynamically, reflecting the relevance of each slot to the current input. The CMN leverages this context-aware memory representation to improve performance in tasks requiring nuanced understanding and long-term dependency modeling. The resulting architecture demonstrates enhanced ability to prioritize relevant information within the memory, leading to improved accuracy and efficiency. The key innovation is the integration of a learnable attention layer that adapts to the input context, moving beyond the fixed-weight approaches of traditional MemNets.

title: The Exact KL Radius of Two Bernoulli Products on Three Bits
abstract: Anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed computer-assisted theorem candidate addressing AIM-PROBABILITY-0002. The claimed exact maximum forward-Kullback-Leibler error of the closed RBM(3,1) model, equivalently a mixture of two Bernoulli products on three bits, is -3/4 log(2 sqrt(3)-3) nats (approximately 0.830615532444 bits), attained only by the two uniform parity targets. The package contains the 11-page manuscript, analytic lower bound and continuous support/channel reduction, six exact convex-cover certificates with 16,600 leaves and 93,792 vertex conditions, a standard-library verifier, adversarial tests, a rational target-to-feasible-witness interface, and an elementary nonsharp conditioning upper bound for specified higher-dimensional product-mixture budgets. It also includes the review response and five producer-coordinated internal editorial reports. The exact Stage-1 review target is preserved as a separate ZIP. SHA256SUMS.txt binds the three substantive assets. The constant and conditioning principle have explicitly cited prior antecedents. Finite diagnostics, producer replay, CI and internal model review are not unaffiliated mathematical validation. No general optimal-projection algorithm, higher-dimensional sharpness, general larger-RBM equivalence, exhaustive novelty, formal verification, external peer review or four-star impact is claimed. Original manuscript, certificate data and editorial material: CC0. Original executable code: MIT, as specified in LICENSE-CODE. Third-party papers, supplied-review text and other NOASSERTION material are not redistributed. Publisher: Evidence Press.

title: Dynamic Topological Dependency Semantic Networks (DTSSN)
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Topological Dependency Semantic Networks (DTSSN), a novel approach to predicting and interpreting complex system behavior. Traditional knowledge representation methods often struggle with the inherent dynamism and intricate dependencies found in complex systems. DTSSN addresses this limitation by constructing a continuously evolving knowledge graph that explicitly models topological relationships and dynamic semantic associations. The core of the system lies in its "living graph" methodology, where nodes represent system components or concepts, and edges represent dependencies and semantic relationships (such as causality, influence, or similarity). The graph's topology adapts in real-time based on system state and events, coupled with a "semantic flow" mechanism to capture dynamic changes in these relationships. This semantic flow leverages deep learning models, specifically Variational Autoencoders (VAE) or Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), to learn and represent semantic associations and propagate them through the graph based on topological information. Prediction and interpretation are then achieved through graph-based reasoning, employing techniques like Reinforcement Learning or Causal Inference algorithms for decision-making and scenario simulation. DTSSN's innovation lies in its ability to move beyond static knowledge representation, offering a dynamic framework to analyze and anticipate behavior in systems exhibiting non-linearity, high dimensionality, and temporal evolution.

title: Interpretable Deep Learning Models with Causal Reasoning
abstract: This paper investigates the integration of causal reasoning into interpretable deep learning models. Current interpretable models often rely on statistical correlations, which can be misleading and lack true understanding. We propose a novel approach that leverages causal graphs and causal rules to guide the training of deep learning models, ensuring that learned relationships are genuinely causal. This method aims to enhance both the interpretability and trustworthiness of these models. We introduce a framework where causal inference is explicitly incorporated into the model architecture and training process. The core claim is that by embedding causal reasoning, we can significantly improve the explanatory power and reliability of interpretable deep learning models. We explore the mechanisms involved in translating causal knowledge into actionable model adjustments. This work contributes to a more robust and reliable approach to AI, particularly in domains where understanding the underlying causal mechanisms is paramount. The ultimate goal is to develop models that not only predict accurately but also provide transparent and trustworthy explanations for their decisions. ---

title: Quantum Topology Information Generation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum topology information generation method, leveraging the unique properties of quantum topology to create quantum states with specific attributes, enabling quantum information encoding and transmission. The core mechanism centers on manipulating quantum geometry to generate tailored quantum states, offering a fundamentally different approach to quantum data manipulation and secure communication. The study explores the potential of this technique, demonstrating the generation of entangled states exhibiting specific topological features, potentially opening avenues for advanced quantum technologies.

title: EraGene Knowledge Graph
abstract: EraGene Knowledge Graph This repository contains the annotations used to build the EraGene knowledge graph. The database is provided as a Neo4j dump (Version 2026.06.0), which can be easily imported into a Neo4j instance. Once imported, the database can be explored by querying it using the Cypher query language. The following sections provide instructions and examples for interacting with the database. Requeriments Download and install Neo4j for Desktop 2.2.1 or later here. Create an instance if none is available. Getting started Download the Dump File Download the database dump file (eragene.dump). Save it to a suitable location on your local machine. Prepare the Database Run Neo4j Desktop. Stop the instance if it is running (important). Identify the path where the instance is stored. Example for windows: Path = C:\Users\user\.Neo4jDesktop2\Data\dbmss\dbms-xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxxx Load the Database Run the following command to load the dump file and populate the database. {Path}/bin/neo4j-admin database load neo4j --from-path=/path/to/dump/eragene.dump --overwrite-destination=true Replace {Path} with the path to your Neo4j instance's directory. If no errors occur, the database has been successfully imported. CALL db.schema.visualization(); Node Properties The nodes that constitute the graph database are described in the following table. title: Non-linear Geometry-Physical Modeling
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for modeling complex systems utilizing a non-linear geometric model. We propose a system that integrates geometric principles with physical processes, allowing for predictive capabilities and providing a foundation for quantum computation. The core claim is that this model, built through a non-linear geometric framework, can accurately simulate physical behavior and offer new theoretical insights for quantum computing. The research explores the potential of leveraging geometric properties to enhance the fidelity and interpretability of quantum computations.

title: High-Order Quantum Entanglement Computation Models
abstract: This research explores the development of novel computational models predicated on high-order quantum entanglement, aiming to significantly enhance the efficiency and scalability of quantum computation. Traditional approaches often struggle to effectively utilize the unique properties of entangled states, necessitating innovative modeling strategies. This work proposes a framework leveraging these properties to enable complex quantum computations, pushing the boundaries of what is currently achievable with existing quantum hardware. The core mechanism centers on dynamically generating and manipulating entangled states, facilitating algorithms with enhanced expressiveness and reduced resource requirements. The resulting models offer a pathway to overcome limitations inherent in current quantum algorithms.

title: Quantum States of Self-Organizing Information Fields
abstract: Quantum information fields are fundamentally different from classical information fields, exhibiting unique properties that enable novel computational paradigms. This paper explores the concept of self-organizing information fields – a theoretical framework that posits the existence of patterns and structures within these fields that drive their dynamic behavior. We investigate the potential of leveraging these self-organizing characteristics to design a quantum algorithm that surpasses current limitations in quantum computation and data transmission. The core mechanism centers around identifying and exploiting specific patterns within these fields to generate highly efficient and rapid data transfer. The investigation begins with a conceptual analysis of self-organization, progresses through a proposed quantum algorithm architecture, and ultimately details the anticipated benefits of this approach. This work seeks to contribute to the advancement of quantum information processing by demonstrating a viable path towards more powerful and versatile quantum technologies.

title: 混沌域优化
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to optimization, termed "Chaos Domain Optimization," that leverages the inherent properties of chaotic domains to generate global optimum solutions. Traditional optimization techniques often struggle with finding truly optimal solutions, particularly for complex, high-dimensional problems. This research proposes a method that dynamically maps the optimization problem to a chaotic domain, effectively mimicking the self-organization and sensitivity to initial conditions found in chaotic systems. We detail the algorithm's methodology, its mathematical foundation, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness compared to conventional methods. The core innovation lies in the intelligent mapping process, which aims to capture the essential dynamics of the problem within the chaotic domain, enabling the discovery of more robust and globally optimal solutions. This work contributes to the field of optimization by providing a fundamentally new approach that potentially overcomes limitations of existing methods.

The core innovation lies in the intelligent mapping process, which aims to capture the essential dynamics of the problem within the chaotic domain, enabling the discovery of more robust and globally optimal solutions. This work contributes to the field of optimization by providing a fundamentally new approach that potentially overcomes limitations of existing methods.

title: Cognitive Graph Embeddings with Hierarchical Abstraction
abstract: Existing graph embedding techniques primarily focus on capturing low-level relationships within a graph, often failing to represent the higher-level, hierarchical structures that are fundamental to human cognition. This paper proposes a novel approach to graph embeddings – Cognitive Graph Embeddings (CGEs) – which explicitly incorporates hierarchical abstraction. CGEs utilize a multi-layered graph representation where nodes are organized into levels of granularity, mirroring the way humans understand and process information. The core mechanism involves learning embeddings for nodes at each layer, allowing for the representation of concepts at varying levels of abstraction. We introduce a framework for constructing these layered graphs and a corresponding embedding method that leverages both local and global graph information. The key innovation lies in the explicit modeling of hierarchical relationships, leading to embeddings that better reflect cognitive structures and potentially improving performance in downstream tasks that require understanding of complex relationships. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CGEs through a conceptual framework and discuss its potential applications in areas such as knowledge representation, reasoning, and recommendation systems.
